title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 140 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 665–674 (Night 140, continuing directly from nights-139), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 140 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. King Sāsān hangs an emir for speaking up for Kān Mā Kān, then repents and sends Turkāsh with a hundred horsemen to search for him, in vain. Kān Mā Kān wanders the wilderness and at night hears a lovesick voice reciting verse: it is Ṣabbāḥ ibn Rammāḥ, a young Bedouin who cannot pay the bride-price his uncle demands for his cousin Najma and means to rob merchants outside Baghdad. Ṣabbāḥ tries to take Kān Mā Kān captive, is thrown in a wrestling bout and beaten again with sword against shield, and swears to be his companion before going on to Baghdad. Alone, Kān Mā Kān prays for provision, and a dying rider comes up on a wonderful horse: Ghassān, a horse-thief, who followed the old woman Dhāt al-Dawāhī from Constantinople to steal it and met fifty highwaymen under Kahrdāsh. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمُوفِيَةُ لِلْأَرْبَعِينَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mūfiyatu li-al-arbaʿīna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing for the forty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fortieth night,
sentences.n: al-mūfiya, “the completing one”, is the active participle of awfā, “to make up the full measure”: this is the night that brings the count to forty after the hundred, the usual way of naming a night that ends in a ten.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ سَاسَانَ وَصَلَ إِلَيْهِ خَبَرُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ مِنَ الْأُمَرَاءِ الْكِبَارِ وَقَالُوا لَهُ إِنَّهُ وَلَدُ مَلِكِنَا وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّةِ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ وَقَدْ بَلَغَنَا أَنَّهُ تَغَرَّبَ عَنِ الْأَوْطَانِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika sāsāna waṣala ilayhi khabaru kāna mā kāna mina al-umarāʾi al-kibāri wa-qālū lahu innahu waladu malikinā wa-min dhurriyyati al-maliki ʿumara bni al-nuʿmāni wa-qad balaghanā annahu tagharraba ʿani al-awṭāni
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that al-Malik Sāsān, there reached him the news of Kān Mā Kān from the emirs the great, and they said to him: Truly he is the son of our king, and of the offspring of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, and it has reached us that he has gone-off-a-stranger from the homelands.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that word of Kān Mā Kān came to al-Malik Sāsān from the great emirs. “He is our king's son,” they told him, “of the line of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, and we hear that he has gone to wander far from home.”
sentences.n: Again the subject is set at the head, al-malik sāsān, and taken up by the pronoun in ilayhi, “reached him”. khabar … min, “news … from”: the emirs are those who bring it. waladu malikinā, “our king's son”: the emirs still call Ḍawʾ al-Makān their king. dhurriyya, “offspring, line”. tagharraba, “to become a stranger, go abroad”; awṭān, plural of waṭan, “homeland”. Rhyme: al-nuʿmān / al-awṭān. The print marks the doubled rāʾ of dhurriyya and of tagharraba (ذرّية, تغرّب).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ سَاسَانُ كَلَامَهُمْ غَضِبَ عَلَيْهِمْ وَأَمَرَ بِشَنْقِ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ وَعَلَّقَهُ فَوَقَعَتْ هَيْبَتُهُ فِي قُلُوبِ بَقِيَّةِ الدَّوْلَةِ وَلَمْ يَقْدِرْ أَحَدٌ مِنْهُمْ أَنْ يَتَكَلَّمَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku sāsānu kalāmahum ghaḍiba ʿalayhim wa-amara bi-shanqi wāḥidin minhum wa-ʿallaqahu fa-waqaʿat haybatuhu fī qulūbi baqiyyati al-dawlati wa-lam yaqdir aḥadun minhum an yatakallama
sentences.l: And when al-Malik Sāsān heard their speech, he grew-angry against them and commanded the hanging of one of them, and he hung him up; and the awe of him fell into the hearts of the rest of the state, and not one of them was able to speak.
sentences.i: When al-Malik Sāsān heard what they said he was angry with them. He ordered one of them hanged, and hanged he was, and dread of him fell on the hearts of all the rest of the court, so that not one of them dared say a word.
sentences.n: amara bi-, “to order”: bi- marks what is ordered. shanq, “hanging”. wa-ʿallaqahu, “and he hung him up”: the king is said to do what his men do at his command. hayba, “awe, the fear that power inspires”. al-dawla, “the state”, here its men, the officers of the court.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ سَاسَانَ تَذَكَّرَ مَا صَنَعَهُ مَعَهُ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ مِنَ الْجَمِيلِ وَأَنَّهُ أَوْصَاهُ بِهِ فَحَزِنَ عَلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ لَابُدَّ مِنَ التَّفْتِيشِ عَلَيْهِ فِي سَائِرِ الْبِلَادِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna sāsāna tadhakkara mā ṣanaʿahu maʿahu ḍawʾu al-makāni mina al-jamīli wa-annahu awṣāhu bihi fa-ḥazina ʿalā kāna mā kāna wa-qāla lā budda mina al-taftīshi ʿalayhi fī sāʾiri al-bilādi
sentences.l: Then Sāsān remembered what Ḍawʾ al-Makān had done with him of the fair-deed, and that he had charged him with him; and he grieved over Kān Mā Kān and said: There is no escape from the searching for him in all the lands.
sentences.i: Then Sāsān remembered the kindness Ḍawʾ al-Makān had shown him, and how he had commended his son to his care; and he grieved for Kān Mā Kān and said, “He must be searched for in every land.”
sentences.n: ṣanaʿa maʿa, “to do with someone”, to treat him. al-jamīl, “the fair thing”, a kindness, a favour. awṣāhu bihi, “he charged him with him”: on his deathbed Ḍawʾ al-Makān left his son in the Chamberlain's care; bi- marks the one entrusted. lā budda min, “there is no escaping”, it must be; the print runs lā into budda (لابد). fattasha ʿalā, “to search for”, is the spoken construction, where Classical prose says fattasha ʿan. sāʾir, “all, the whole of”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ أَحْضَرَ تُرْكَاشَ وَأَمَرَهُ أَنْ يَنْتَخِبَ مِائَةَ فَارِسٍ وَيَأْخُذَهُمْ وَيَدُورَ عَلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu aḥḍara turkāsha wa-amarahu an yantakhiba miʾata fārisin wa-yaʾkhudhahum wa-yadūra ʿalā kāna mā kāna
sentences.l: Then he had Turkāsh brought, and commanded him that he choose a hundred horsemen and take them and go-round after Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: Then he summoned Turkāsh and ordered him to pick out a hundred horsemen, take them with him, and go in search of Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.n: aḥḍara, “to cause to be present”, to summon. Turkāsh is one of the emirs. intakhaba, “to choose, pick out”. dāra ʿalā, “to go round after”, to look for: spoken usage.

sentences.t: فَذَهَبَ وَغَابَ عَشَرَةَ أَيَّامٍ وَرَجَعَ وَقَالَ لَمْ أَطَّلِعْ لَهُ عَلَى خَبَرٍ وَلَا وَقَفْتُ لَهُ عَلَى أَثَرٍ وَلَا أَحَدٌ أَخْبَرَنِي عَنْهُ بِخَبَرٍ
sentences.tr: fa-dhahaba wa-ghāba ʿasharata ayyāmin wa-rajaʿa wa-qāla lam aṭṭaliʿ lahu ʿalā khabarin wa-lā waqaftu lahu ʿalā atharin wa-lā aḥadun akhbaranī ʿanhu bi-khabarin
sentences.l: And he went and was absent ten days, and returned and said: I have not come-to-know for him of any news, nor have I stood for him upon a trace, nor anyone informed me about him with news.
sentences.i: He went off and was gone ten days, and came back and said, “I have learned no news of him and come upon no trace of him, and no one has given me any word of him.”
sentences.n: Rhyme: khabar / athar / khabar. iṭṭalaʿa ʿalā, “to gain knowledge of”; waqafa ʿalā, “to come upon, find”. lahu, “for him”, in both phrases means “of him”, a spoken turn. wa-lā aḥadun akhbaranī, “nor anyone told me”: lā here denies a whole clause with a past verb, more freely than Classical prose allows. akhbara bi-, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news.

sentences.t: فَحَزِنَ الْمَلِكُ سَاسَانُ عَلَى مَا فَعَلَ مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥazina al-maliku sāsānu ʿalā mā faʿala maʿahu
sentences.l: And al-Malik Sāsān grieved over what he had done with him.
sentences.i: And al-Malik Sāsān was sorry for the way he had treated him.
sentences.n: faʿala maʿa, like ṣanaʿa maʿa above, “to deal with someone”: he regrets having had the boy shut out from his cousin.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا أُمُّهُ فَإِنَّهَا صَارَتْ لَايَقِرُّلَهَا قَرَارٌ وَلَايُطَاوِعُهَا اصْطِبَارٌ وَمَضَي عَلَيْهَا عِشْرُونَ يَوْمًا كِبَارًا
sentences.tr: wa-ammā ummuhu fa-innahā ṣārat lā yaqirru lahā qarārun wa-lā yuṭāwiʿuhā iṣṭibārun wa-maḍā ʿalayhā ʿishrūna yawman kibāran
sentences.l: And as for his mother, she became (such that) there does not settle for her a settling, nor does patience obey her; and there passed over her twenty days, great-ones.
sentences.i: As for his mother, she could find no rest, and patience would not come at her call; and twenty long days went by over her.
sentences.n: Rhyme: qarār / iṣṭibār. lā yaqirru lahā qarārun, “no settling settles for her”, a stock phrase for restlessness; iṣṭibār, “patience, holding oneself in”. The print runs lā into the verbs and yaqirru into lahā (لايقرلها, لايطاوعها), spells maḍā with a dotted yāʾ (مضي), and marks the doubled mīm of ummuhu (امّه). ʿishrūna yawman kibāran, “twenty great days”, long and heavy ones: the adjective goes by the sense, plural, though the counted noun is singular.

sentences.t: فَهٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ هٰؤُلَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-hādhā mā kāna min amri hāʾulāʾi
sentences.l: So this is what was of the affair of these.
sentences.i: So much for them.
sentences.n: The storyteller's formula for laying down one thread of the tale and taking up another.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَإِنَّهُ لَمَّا خَرَجَ مِنْ بَغْدَادَ صَارَ مُتَحَيِّرًا فِي أَمْرِهِ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ أَيْنَ يَرُوحُ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri kāna mā kāna fa-innahu lammā kharaja min baghdāda ṣāra mutaḥayyiran fī amrihi wa-lam yaʿlam ayna yarūḥu
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of Kān Mā Kān, truly he, when he went out from Baghdad, became bewildered in his affair and did not know where he should go.
sentences.i: As for Kān Mā Kān, when he left Baghdad he was at a loss what to do, and did not know where to go.
sentences.n: mā kāna min amri kāna mā kāna, “what was of the affair of Kān Mā Kān”: the formula sits oddly well beside the hero's name, which itself means “what was, was”. mutaḥayyir, “perplexed, at a loss”. rāḥa, yarūḥu, “to go”, is the everyday verb of spoken Arabic.

sentences.t: فَسَارَ فِى الْبَرِّ ثَلٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ وَحْدَةُ فَلَمْ يَرَ رَاجِلًا وَلَا فَارِسًا فَطَارَ رُقَادُةُ وَزَادَ سُهَادُةُ وَتَفَكَّرَ أَهْلَهُ وَبِلَادَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-sāra fī al-barri thalāthata ayyāmin waḥdahu fa-lam yara rājilan wa-lā fārisan fa-ṭāra ruqāduhu wa-zāda suhāduhu wa-tafakkara ahlahu wa-bilādahu
sentences.l: And he went in the open-land three days by himself, and he did not see a man-on-foot nor a horseman; and his sleep flew, and his sleeplessness increased, and he called-to-mind his people and his country.
sentences.i: For three days he journeyed alone through the open country and saw no one on foot or on horseback. Sleep fled from him, his wakefulness grew, and he thought of his family and his homeland.
sentences.n: barr, “land”, the open country away from towns and water; the print marks its doubled rāʾ (البرّ), writes fī with a dotless yāʾ (فى), and spells thalātha without its long alif (ثلثة), which the small alif supplies. It also writes the pronoun -hu with tāʾ marbūṭa in waḥdahu, ruqāduhu, suhāduhu and bilādahu (وحدة, رقادة, سهادة, بلادة); read -hu. Rhyme: ruqāduhu / suhāduhu / bilādahu. ruqād, “sleep”; suhād, “sleeplessness”. tafakkara, “to think of”, takes its object directly, as in the spoken language.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ يَتَقَوَّتُ مِنْ نَبَاتِ الْأَرْضِ وَيَشْرَبُ مِنْ أَنْهَارِهَا وَيَقِيلُ وَقْتَ الْحَرِّ فِي كُلِّ قَائِلَةٍ تَحْتَ أَشْجَارِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra yataqawwatu min nabāti al-arḍi wa-yashrabu min anhārihā wa-yaqīlu waqta al-ḥarri fī kulli qāʾilatin taḥta ashjārihā
sentences.l: And he took-to feeding-himself from the plants of the earth, and drinking from its rivers, and taking-the-noon-rest at the time of the heat, in every noontide, under its trees.
sentences.i: He lived on the plants of the earth and drank from its streams, and in the heat of every noon he rested under its trees.
sentences.n: The print has ينقوت, a misprint for يتقوت, corrected here; the same verb is printed rightly a few lines on. taqawwata min, “to feed oneself on”; qūt, “food enough to live on”. qāla, yaqīlu, “to take the midday rest”; qāʾila, “the noontide, the siesta”. Rhyme: anhārihā / ashjārihā. The print marks the doubled rāʾ of al-ḥarr (الحرّ).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَ مِنْ تِلْكَ الطَّرِيقِ إِلَى طَرِيقٍ أُخْرَى وَسَارَ فِيهَا ثَلٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: thumma kharaja min tilka al-ṭarīqi ilā ṭarīqin ukhrā wa-sāra fīhā thalāthata ayyāmin
sentences.l: Then he went out from that road to another road, and went in it three days.
sentences.i: Then he left that road for another, and followed it for three days.
sentences.n: ṭarīq, “road”, is feminine here (tilka, ukhrā, fīhā), as it may be in both Classical and spoken usage.

sentences.t: وَفِى الْيَوْمِ الرَّابِعِ أَشْرَفَ عَلَى أَرْضٍ مُعْشِبَةِ الْفَلَوَاتِ مُخَضَّبَةِ النَّبَاتِ مَلِيحَةِ الْجَنَبَاتِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī al-yawmi al-rābiʿi ashrafa ʿalā arḍin muʿshibati al-falawāti mukhaḍḍabati al-nabāti malīḥati al-janabāti
sentences.l: And on the day the fourth he looked-down upon a land grassy of the wastes, dyed of the plants, comely of the sides.
sentences.i: On the fourth day he came out above a land whose open spaces were deep in grass, its plants as bright as if dyed, and fair on every side.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: al-falawāt / al-nabāt / al-janabāt. ashrafa ʿalā, “to look down on from a height”, to come in sight of. Each adjective is joined to a noun in the genitive, “grassy of wastes”, meaning “whose wastes are grassy”. falāt, plural falawāt, “open waterless country”; janabāt, “sides, flanks”. mukhaḍḍaba, “dyed”, is read as the passive participle of khaḍḍaba, “to dye, tint”, the plants as vivid as hennaed hands; it may instead be a misprint for mukhṣiba, “fertile” (مخصبة, one dot different), which would pair neatly with muʿshiba, but it is kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَهٰذِةِ الْأَرْضُ قَدْ شَرِبَتْ مِنْ كَأْسَاتِ الْغَمَامِ عَلَى أَصْوَاتِ الرُّعُودِ وَالْحَمَامِ فَاخْضَرَّتْ جَوَانِبُهَا وَطَابَ فَلَاهَا
sentences.tr: wa-hādhihi al-arḍu qad sharibat min kaʾsāti al-ghamāmi ʿalā aṣwāti al-ruʿūdi wa-al-ḥamāmi fa-ikhḍarrat jawānibuhā wa-ṭāba falāhā
sentences.l: And this land had drunk from the cups of the clouds to the voices of the thunders and the doves, so its sides grew-green and its open-ground became-sweet.
sentences.i: This land had drunk from the cups of the clouds to the music of thunder and of doves, so that its slopes were green and its open spaces sweet.
sentences.n: The print spells hādhihi with tāʾ marbūṭa (هذة). Rhyme: al-ghamām / al-ḥamām. kaʾsāt, a plural of kaʾs, “cup”: to drink “to the voices” (ʿalā aṣwāt) of singers is the language of the wine party, here given to the rain. falā, “open country”, beside the plural falawāt above.

sentences.t: فَتَذَكَّرَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ بِلَادَ أَبِيهِ بَغْدَادَ فَأَنْشَدَ مِنْ فَرْطِ مَا هُوَ فِيهِ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-tadhakkara kāna mā kāna bilāda abīhi baghdāda fa-anshada min farṭi mā huwa fīhi yaqūlu
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān remembered the country of his father, Baghdad, and he recited, from the excess of what he was in, saying:
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān remembered his father's city, Baghdad, and from the fullness of his heart he recited:
sentences.n: farṭ, “excess, overflowing”: min farṭi mā huwa fīhi, “from the excess of what he was in”, of the longing he felt. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, the usual lead into verse.

sentences.t:
خَرَجْتُ وَفِي اَمَلِي عَوْدَةٌ * وَلٰكِنَّنِي لَسْتُ اَدْرِي مَتَى
وَشَرَّدْتُ فِي حُبِّ مَنْ لَمْ اَجِدْ * سَبِيلًا اِلَى دَفْعِ مَا قَدْ اَتَى
sentences.tr:
kharajtu wa-fī amalī ʿawdatun * wa-lākinnanī lastu adrī matā
wa-sharradtu fī ḥubbi man lam ajid * sabīlan ilā dafʿi mā qad atā
sentences.l:
I went out, and in my hope (is) a return, * but I do not know when;
and I have strayed in the love of one — I have not found * a way to the warding-off of what has come.
sentences.i:
I went away, and I hope to come back, * though when, I cannot tell;
I wander for love of one, and have found * no way to ward off what befell.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre mutaqārib, rhyming in -tā, copied as the print points them. sharrada is usually “to drive away”; here it must mean “I have wandered off”, as a strong form of sharada, “to stray, run off”, unless the pointing stands for shurridtu, “I have been driven out”. man, “one who”, is left hanging: the second half turns to a fresh clause, “I have found no way to fend off what has come”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِةِ بَكَى ثُمَّ مَسَحَ دُمُوعَهُ وَأَكَلَ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ النَّبَاتِ مَا يَتَقَوَّتُ بِهِ وَتَوَضَّأَ وَصَلَّى مَا فَاتَهُ مِنَ الْفَرَائِضِ فِي هٰذِةِ الْمُدَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi bakā thumma masaḥa dumūʿahu wa-akala min dhālika al-nabāti mā yataqawwatu bihi wa-tawaḍḍaʾa wa-ṣallā mā fātahu mina al-farāʾiḍi fī hādhihi al-muddati
sentences.l: And when he finished from his poetry he wept, then wiped his tears, and ate of that plant-growth what he might feed-himself with, and made-the-ablution and prayed what had passed him of the obligatory-prayers in this period.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses he wept; then he wiped away his tears, ate enough of those plants to keep himself alive, made his ablutions, and prayed the prayers he had missed in all that time.
sentences.n: The print writes “his poetry” with tāʾ marbūṭa for the pronoun (شعرة, read shiʿrihi), and hādhihi again as هذة. taqawwata bi-, “to live on”: bi- marks the food. farāʾiḍ, “the obligatory (prayers)”, the five daily prayers; a missed prayer is made up afterwards, and he has had no water for ablution until now.

sentences.t: وَجَلَسَ يَسْتَرِيحُ ذٰلِكَ الْيَوْمَ بِطُولِهِ فِي ذٰلِكَ الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-jalasa yastarīḥu dhālika al-yawma bi-ṭūlihi fī dhālika al-makāni
sentences.l: And he sat resting that day in its length in that place.
sentences.i: And he sat and rested the whole of that day in that place.
sentences.n: bi-ṭūlihi, “with its length”, all of it.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَاءَ اللَّيْلُ نَامَ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ نَائِمًا إِلَى نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ ثُمَّ انْتَبَهَ فَسَمِعَ صَوْتَ إِنْسَانٍ يَقُولُ هٰذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jāʾa al-laylu nāma wa-lam yazal nāʾiman ilā niṣfi al-layli thumma intabaha fa-samiʿa ṣawta insānin yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And when the night came he slept, and he did not cease sleeping until the half of the night; then he woke, and he heard the voice of a human-being saying these verses:
sentences.i: When night came he slept, and slept on until midnight; then he woke, and heard someone's voice reciting these verses:
sentences.n: lam yazal, “he did not cease”, with a following participle: he went on sleeping. intabaha, “to wake, become alert”. insān, “a human being”, someone. hādhihi is spelt هذة once more. jāʾa: the print gives the verb its hamza (جاء).

sentences.t:
مَا الْعَيْشُ اِلَّا اَنْ يَرَى لَكَ بَارِقُ * مِنْ ثَغْرِ مَنْ تَهْوَى وَوَجْهٌ رَائِقُ
صَلُّوْا عَلَيْهَا فِي الدُّيُوْرِ اَسَاقِفٌ * خَرُّوْا اِلَيْهَا بِالسُّجُوْدِ تُسَابِقُ
وَالْمَوْتُ اَسْهَلُ مِنْ صُدُوْدِ حَبِيْبِهِ * لَمْ يَغْشَنِي مِنْهَا خَيَالٌ طَارِقُ
يَافَرْحَةَ النُّدَمَاءِ حَيْثُ تَجَمَّعُوْا * وَاَقَامَ مَعْشُوْقٌ هُنَاكَ وَعَاشِقُ
لَاسِيَّمَا وَقْتَ الرَّبِيْعِ وَزَهْرِهِ * طَابَ الزَّمَانُ بِمَا اِلَيْهِ تُسَابِقُ
يَا شَارِبَ الصَّهْبَاءِ دُوْنَكَ هٰذِهِ * اَرْضَ النَّعِيْمِ وَمَاؤُهَا يَتَدَفَّقُ
sentences.tr:
mā al-ʿayshu illā an yarā laka bāriqu * min thaghri man tahwā wa-wajhun rāʾiqu
ṣallū ʿalayhā fī al-duyūri asāqifun * kharrū ilayhā bi-al-sujūdi tusābiqu
wa-al-mawtu ashalu min ṣudūdi ḥabībihi * lam yaghshanī minhā khayālun ṭāriqu
yā farḥata al-nudamāʾi ḥaythu tajammaʿū * wa-aqāma maʿshūqun hunāka wa-ʿāshiqu
lā siyyamā waqta al-rabīʿi wa-zahrihi * ṭāba al-zamānu bi-mā ilayhi tusābiqu
yā shāriba al-ṣahbāʾi dūnaka hādhihi * arḍa al-naʿīmi wa-māʾuhā yatadaffaqu
sentences.i:
Life is nothing but to see a flash of lightning * from the lips you love, and a face clear and bright;
bishops have prayed to her in their monasteries, * and fallen down before her, vying to bow first.
Death is easier than a beloved who turns away; * no phantom of her has come to me by night.
O the joy of boon companions where they meet, * and lover and beloved linger there,
above all in spring, in the season of flowers! * The time is sweet with what you hasten toward.
O drinker of the red wine, here it is before you: * the land of delight, and its waters flowing.
sentences.n: Six lines in the metre kāmil, rhyming in -iqu, copied as the print points them; the last line ends instead in -aqu (yatadaffaqu), a loose rhyme. In the first line the print points yarā, “he sees”, with bāriqu as its subject; the sense wants yurā, “be seen”. bāriq, “a flash of lightning”: the gleam of white teeth in the beloved's mouth (thaghr). In the second line the verb ṣallū is plural before its plural subject asāqif, “bishops”, as in spoken Arabic, and the print gives asāqif a tanwīn the Classical word does not take; tusābiqu, “vying”, is feminine singular with them. Even Christian clergy worship her, a stock hyperbole. ṣudūd, “turning away, aloofness”; the poem slips from “his beloved” to “me”. khayāl ṭāriq, “a night-visiting phantom”: the dream image of the beloved that comes to the lover in sleep. nudamāʾ, plural of nadīm, “boon companion, drinking friend”. lā siyyamā, “especially”. ṣahbāʾ, “wine with a reddish tinge”. dūnaka, “before you”, is also “here, take it”; arḍa al-naʿīmi is accusative, as what is offered.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ هٰذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ هَاجَتْ بِهِ الْأَشْجَانُ وَجَرَتْ دُمُوعُهُ عَلَى خَدِّهِ كَالْغُدْرَانِ وَانْطَلَقَ فِي قَلْبِهِ لَهِيبُ النِّيرَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kāna mā kāna hādhihi al-abyāta hājat bihi al-ashjānu wa-jarat dumūʿuhu ʿalā khaddihi ka-al-ghudrāni wa-inṭalaqa fī qalbihi lahību al-nīrāni
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān heard these verses, the griefs were-stirred-up in him, and his tears ran on his cheek like the pools, and the flame of the fires was let-loose in his heart.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān heard these verses, all his sorrows rose up in him; his tears ran down his cheek in streams, and a blaze of fire broke out in his heart.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: ashjān, ghudrān, nīrān. hājat bihi al-ashjān, “the griefs surged in him”: hāja, “to be stirred up, to rise”. ghudrān, plural of ghadīr, a pool left behind by a flood.

sentences.t: وَقَامَ يَنْظُرُ قَائِلَ هٰذَا الْكَلَامِ فَلَمْ يَرَ أَحَدًا فِي جُنْحِ الظَّلَامِ فَزَادَ وَجْدُةُ وَفَزِعَ وَأَخَذَةُ الْقَلَقُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāma yanẓuru qāʾila hādhā al-kalāmi fa-lam yara aḥadan fī junḥi al-ẓalāmi fa-zāda wajduhu wa-faziʿa wa-akhadhahu al-qalaqu
sentences.l: And he rose looking-for the sayer of these words, but he did not see anyone in the wing of the darkness; so his passion increased, and he took-fright, and the unrest seized him.
sentences.i: He rose to look for whoever had spoken these words, but could see no one in the dark of night; his longing grew, fear came over him, and he could not rest.
sentences.n: Rhyme: kalām, ẓalām. naẓara, “to look”, here takes its object directly: “to look for”. junḥ al-ẓalām, “the wing of the darkness”, the depth of night. wajd, “passion, love-longing”. وجدة and واخذة are wajduhu and akhadhahu, ة for -hu again.

sentences.t: وَنَزَلَ مِنْ مَكَانِهِ إِلَى أَسْفَلِ الْوَادِي وَمَشَى عَلَى شَاطِئِ النَّهْرِ فَسَمِعَ صَاحِبَ الصَّوْتِ يُصَعِّدُ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَيَقُولُ هٰذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-nazala min makānihi ilā asfali al-wādī wa-mashā ʿalā shāṭiʾi al-nahri fa-samiʿa ṣāḥiba al-ṣawti yuṣaʿʿidu al-zafarāti wa-yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta shiʿrun
sentences.l: And he went-down from his place to the bottom of the valley, and walked on the bank of the river; and he heard the owner of the voice sending-up the sighs and saying these verses — poetry:
sentences.i: He came down from where he stood to the floor of the valley and walked along the riverbank, and he heard the owner of the voice heaving sighs and reciting these verses:
sentences.n: ṣāḥib al-ṣawt, “the owner of the voice”: the singer he cannot see. yuṣaʿʿidu al-zafarāt, “sending up the sighs”, the phrase used of his mother in the night before. shiʿr, “poetry”, is the print's heading for the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
اِنْ كُنْتَ تَضْمُرُهَا فِي الْحُبِّ اِشْفَاقًا * فَاَطْلِقِ الدَّمْعَ يَوْمَ الْبَيْنِ اِطْلَاقَا
بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ اَحِبَّائِي عُهُودُ هَوًى * لِذَا اِلَيْهِمْ اَظَلُّ الدَّهْرَ مُشْتَاقًا
يَرْتَاحُ قَلْبِي اِلَيْهِمْ ثُمَّ يُطْرِبُنِي * نَسِيمُ بَرْدٍ اِذَا مَا هَبَّ اَشْوَاقًا
يَا سَعْدُ هَلْ رَبَّةُ الْخَلْخَالِ تَذْكُرُ لِي * بَعْدَ الْبِعَادِ لَنَا عَهْدًا وَمِيثَاقًا
وَهَلْ تَعُودُ لَيَالِي الْوَصْلِ تَجْمَعُنَا * يَوْمًا وَيَشْرَحُ كُلٌّ بَعْضَ مَا لَاقَا
قَالَتْ فُتِنْتَ بِنَا وَجْدًا فَقُلْتُ لَهَا * كَمْ قَدْ فَتَنْتِ رَعَاكِ اللّٰهُ عُشَّاقَا
لَا مَتَّعَ اللّٰهُ طَرْفِي مِنْ مَحَاسِنِهَا * اِنْ كَانَ مِنْ بَعْدِهَا طِيبَ الْكَرَى ذَاقًا
يَا لَسْعَةً فِي فُؤَادِي مَارَايْتُ لَهَا * سِوَى الْوِصَالِ وَرَشْفِ الثَّغْرِ تِرْيَاقًا
sentences.tr:
in kunta taḍmuruhā fī al-ḥubbi ishfāqan * fa-aṭliqi al-damʿa yawma al-bayni iṭlāqā
baynī wa-bayna aḥibbāʾī ʿuhūdu hawan * li-dhā ilayhim aẓallu al-dahra mushtāqā
yartāḥu qalbī ilayhim thumma yuṭribunī * nasīmu bardin idhā mā habba ashwāqā
yā saʿdu hal rabbatu al-khalkhāli tadhkuru lī * baʿda al-biʿādi lanā ʿahdan wa-mīthāqā
wa-hal taʿūdu layālī al-waṣli tajmaʿunā * yawman wa-yashraḥu kullun baʿḍa mā lāqā
qālat futinta binā wajdan fa-qultu lahā * kam qad fatanti raʿāki allāhu ʿushshāqā
lā mattaʿa allāhu ṭarfī min maḥāsinihā * in kāna min baʿdihā ṭība al-karā dhāqā
yā lasʿatan fī fuʾādī mā raʾaytu lahā * siwā al-wiṣāli wa-rashfi al-thaghri tiryāqā
sentences.l:
If you are hiding it in the love out-of-fear, * then let-loose the tears on the day of the parting, a letting-loose.
Between me and between my loved-ones (are) covenants of passion; * for this, toward them I remain the time longing.
My heart takes-ease toward them; then there moves me * a breeze of coolness, whenever it blows, (to) longings.
O Saʿd, does the mistress of the anklet remember for me, * after the distance, a covenant to us and a pact?
And will the nights of the union return, gathering us * one day, and each explain some of what he met?
She said: You are enchanted by us in passion. And I said to her: * How many, God guard you, have you enchanted (of) lovers!
May God not give-enjoyment-to my eye of her beauties * if, after her, it has tasted the sweetness of the sleep.
O for a sting in my heart! I have not seen for it, * other than the union and the sipping of the mouth, an antidote.
sentences.i:
If for fear you hide your love away, * then on the day of parting let your tears run free.
Between me and those I love are vows of passion, * and so I long for them as long as time endures.
My heart takes comfort, turning toward them, and a cool * breeze, whenever it blows, stirs me to longing.
O Saʿd, does the lady of the anklet still recall, * now we are far apart, our promise and our pact?
Will the nights of union come again and bring us * together one day, for each to tell some part of what he bore?
She said, “You are bewitched by me with longing.” I told her, * “God keep you, how many lovers have you bewitched!”
May God never let my eye delight in her beauty * if, since she went, it has tasted the sweetness of sleep.
Ah, for this sting in my heart! I have found no antidote * for it but union, and to sip from her lips.
sentences.n: Eight lines in the metre basīṭ, rhyming in -āqā, copied as the print points them. The print points taḍmuruhā; the sense wants tuḍmiruhā, “you hide it”, from aḍmara, “to conceal”, and “it” is the love itself. ishfāq, “fear, anxious care”. bayn, “parting”. li-dhā, “for this reason”. aṭraba, “to move to delight” or, as here, to stirring emotion; ashwāqan, “(to) longings”, names what the breeze stirs in him. Saʿd is the stock companion a lover calls on in Arabic verse. khalkhāl, “anklet”: rabbat al-khalkhāl, “she of the anklet”, is the beloved. lāqā is written with a plain alif (لاقا) for the usual لاقى. The print sets tanwīn on the verb dhāqa, “it tasted” (ذَاقًا), as if it were one of the accusative rhyme words around it; a verb takes no tanwīn, and the reading is dhāqā. karā, “sleep”. The print runs mā raʾaytu together (مارايت) and writes raʾaytu without its hamza. lasʿa, the sting of a scorpion or the bite of a snake; tiryāq, “theriac, antidote”; rashf al-thaghr, “sipping the mouth”, is kissing.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ هٰذِةِ الْأَشْعَارَ مِنْ صَاحِبِ ذٰلِكَ الصَّوْتِ ثَانِيَ مَرَّةٍ وَلَمْ يَرَ شَخْصَهُ عَلِمَ أَنَّ ذٰلِكَ الْقَائِلَ عَاشِقٌ مِثْلُهُ وَمُنِعَ مِنَ الْوَصْلِ إِلَى مَنْ يُحِبُّهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kāna mā kāna hādhihi al-ashʿāra min ṣāḥibi dhālika al-ṣawti thāniya marratin wa-lam yara shakhṣahu ʿalima anna dhālika al-qāʾila ʿāshiqun mithluhu wa-muniʿa mina al-waṣli ilā man yuḥibbuhu
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān heard these poems from the owner of that voice a second time, and did not see his person, he knew that that sayer (was) a lover like-him, and (had been) prevented from the reaching to whom he loves.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān heard these verses from the owner of that voice a second time and still could not see him, he knew that the speaker was a lover like himself, kept from the one he loved.
sentences.n: thāniya marratin, “a second time”. mithluhu, “like him”, takes the case of the word it describes, here ʿāshiqun. muniʿa, “he was prevented”, is passive. al-waṣl ilā, “reaching, attaining to”: union with the beloved. The print marks the doubled letters of marra and yuḥibbuhu.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ هٰذَا يَصْلُحُ أَنْ يَضَعَ رَأْسَهُ إِلَى رَأْسِي وَأَجْعَلُهُ أَنِيسًالِي فِي هٰذِةِ الْغُرْبَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla fī nafsihi hādhā yaṣluḥu an yaḍaʿa raʾsahu ilā raʾsī wa-ajʿaluhu anīsan lī fī hādhihi al-ghurbati
sentences.l: And he said in himself: This (one) is-fit that he put his head to my head, and I make him a companion for me in this exile.
sentences.i: He said to himself, “Here is a man fit to lay his head beside mine. I will make him my companion in this exile.”
sentences.n: yaḍaʿa raʾsahu ilā raʾsī, “put his head to my head”: to be a close companion, sharing one's rest and one's troubles. The print writes raʾs without its hamza (راس) and runs anīsan lī together (انيسالي). wa-ajʿaluhu, “and I will make him”, turns from what the man is fit for to what Kān Mā Kān means to do; it could also be read wa-ajʿalahu, carried on from an yaḍaʿa: “fit … that I make him”. ghurba, “being far from home, exile”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَنَحْنَحَ وَنَادَى قَائِلًا أَيُّهَا السَّائِرُ فِى اللَّيْلِ الْعَاكِرِ تَقَرَّبْ مِنِّي وَقُصَّ عَلَيَّ قِصَّتَكَ لَعَلَّكَ أَنْ تَجِدَنِي مُعِينًا لَكَ عَلَى بَلِيَّتِكَ
sentences.tr: thumma tanaḥnaḥa wa-nādā qāʾilan ayyuhā al-sāʾiru fī al-layli al-ʿākiri taqarrab minnī wa-quṣṣa ʿalayya qiṣṣataka laʿallaka an tajidanī muʿīnan laka ʿalā baliyyatika
sentences.l: Then he cleared-his-throat and called, saying: O you the traveller in the night, the murky, come-near to me and relate to me your story; perhaps you, that you find me a helper for you against your affliction.
sentences.i: Then he cleared his throat and called out, “You who travel through this murky night, come closer and tell me your story; you may find in me someone to help you bear your trouble.”
sentences.n: tanaḥnaḥa, “to clear one's throat”, the polite noise that announces one's presence. al-ʿākir, “murky”, of a night thick with darkness; the same root returns in bi-al-iʿtikār below. laʿallaka an tajidanī, “perhaps you, that you find me”: an after laʿalla is a later turn that Classical usage does without. baliyya, “affliction, trial”. The print marks the doubled letters of taqarrab, quṣṣa, ʿalayya, laʿallaka and baliyyatika, and writes fī with a dotless yāʾ (فى).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ صَاحِبُ الصَّوْتِ ذٰلِكَ الْكَلَامَ نَادَى أَيُّهَا الْمُجِيبُ لِدَعْوَتِي وَالسَّامِعُ لِقِصَّتِي مَنْ تَكُونُ مِنَ الْفُرْسَانِ وَهَلْ أَنْتَ مِنَ الْإِنْسِ أَوِ الْجَانِّ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ṣāḥibu al-ṣawti dhālika al-kalāma nādā ayyuhā al-mujību li-daʿwatī wa-al-sāmiʿu li-qiṣṣatī man takūnu mina al-fursāni wa-hal anta mina al-insi awi al-jānni
sentences.l: And when the owner of the voice heard those words, he called: O you the answerer to my call, and the hearer to my story, who are you of the horsemen? And are you of the humankind or the jinn?
sentences.i: When the owner of the voice heard this, he called back, “You who answer my call and would hear my story, which of the knights are you? And are you a man, or one of the jinn?”
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: daʿwatī, qiṣṣatī; fursān, jānn (in pause, jān). al-mujīb li-, al-sāmiʿ li-, “the answerer to, the hearer to”: li- marks the object of the participle. man takūnu, “who might you be?”. al-ins and al-jinn (here al-jānn) are the two kinds of being that God made with reason, mankind and the jinn.

sentences.t: عَجِّلْ عَلَيَّ بِكَلَامِكَ قَبْلَ دُنُوِّ حِمَامِكَ فَإِنَّ لِي سَائِرًا فِي هٰذِهِ الْبَرِّيَّةِ نَحْوَ عِشْرِينَ يَوْمًا فَلَمْ أَرَ شَخْصًا وَلَمْ أَسْمَعْ صَوْتًا غَيْرَ صَوْتِكَ
sentences.tr: ʿajjil ʿalayya bi-kalāmika qabla dunuwwi ḥimāmika fa-inna lī sāʾiran fī hādhihi al-barriyyati naḥwa ʿishrīna yawman fa-lam ara shakhṣan wa-lam asmaʿ ṣawtan ghayra ṣawtika
sentences.l: Hasten upon me with your speech before the drawing-near of your death, for to me, travelling in this wilderness, (are) about twenty days, and I have not seen a person nor heard a voice other than your voice.
sentences.i: Answer me quickly, before your death draws near; for I have been travelling through this wilderness some twenty days, and in all that time I have seen no one and heard no voice but yours.
sentences.n: Rhyme: kalāmika, ḥimāmika. ḥimām, “the fated hour of death”: a warning, in case the stranger is an enemy or a jinn. ʿajjil ʿalayya bi-, “hurry to me with”. fa-inna lī sāʾiran … naḥwa ʿishrīna yawman, “for I have been travelling some twenty days”, is a colloquial turn put into the shape of an inna sentence: lī with a length of time, “I have twenty days (at it)”, as in the spoken lī ʿishrīn yōm, with sāʾiran left in the accusative after inna. barriyya, “open country, wilderness”. Here the print spells hādhihi in the usual way (هذه).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ قَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ هٰذَا قِصَّتُهُ مِثْلُ قِصَّتِي فَإِنِّي أَنَا الْآخَرُ لِي أَيْضًا عِشْرُونَ يَوْمًا وَأَنَا سَائِرٌ لَمْ أَرَ شَخْصًا وَلَا أَسْمَعُ صَوْتًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kāna mā kāna hādhā al-kalāma qāla fī nafsihi hādhā qiṣṣatuhu mithlu qiṣṣatī fa-innī anā al-ākharu lī ayḍan ʿishrūna yawman wa-anā sāʾirun lam ara shakhṣan wa-lā asmaʿu ṣawtan
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān heard these words, he said in himself: This (one), his story (is) like my story; for I, I the other, to me also (are) twenty days and I travelling; I have not seen a person nor do I hear a voice.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān heard this, he said to himself, “This man's story is the same as mine: I too have been travelling for twenty days without seeing a soul or hearing a voice.”
sentences.n: hādhā qiṣṣatuhu, “this one, his story”: the man is set at the head of the sentence and taken up again by the pronoun. anā al-ākhar, “I the other”, is a colloquial “I too” (Egyptian ana kamān, ana al-ākhar), and ayḍan, “also”, says it again. lī … ʿishrūna yawman, “I have twenty days”, is the same turn the stranger used. lam ara … wa-lā asmaʿu: the first verb is negated with lam, the second with a plain lā and left in the present, a loose pairing.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَمْ أَرُدَّ عَلَيْهِ جَوَابًا حَتَّى يَطْلُعَ النَّهَارُ ثُمَّ سَكَتَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla fī nafsihi lam arudda ʿalayhi jawāban ḥattā yaṭluʿa al-nahāru thumma sakata
sentences.l: And he said in himself: I did not return to him an answer until the day rises. Then he was-silent.
sentences.i: And he said to himself, “I will give him no answer until daylight comes,” and he kept silent.
sentences.n: lam arudda, “I did not answer”, stands for lan arudda, “I will not answer”: lam for lan is a Middle Arabic habit, and ḥattā yaṭluʿa al-nahāru, “until the day rises”, shows that the future is meant. radda ʿalayhi jawāban, “to give him back an answer”.

sentences.t: فَنَادَاهُ صَاحِبُ الصَّوْتِ أَيُّهَا الدَّاعِي إِنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الْجَانِّ فَاذْهَبْ بِسَلَامٍ وَإِنْ كُنْتَ إِنْسِيًّا فَالْبَثْ مَلِيًّا حَتَّى يَطْلُعَ الْفَجْرُ وَالنَّهَارُ وَيَذْهَبَ اللَّيْلُ بِالِاعْتِكَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-nādāhu ṣāḥibu al-ṣawti ayyuhā al-dāʿī in kunta mina al-jānni fa-idhhab bi-salāmin wa-in kunta insiyyan fa-ilbath maliyyan ḥattā yaṭluʿa al-fajru wa-al-nahāru wa-yadhhaba al-laylu bi-al-iʿtikāri
sentences.l: And the owner of the voice called him: O you the caller, if you are of the jinn, then go in peace; and if you are human, then tarry a-long-while, until the dawn and the day rise and the night goes with the darkness.
sentences.i: Then the owner of the voice called to him, “You who called out to me: if you are of the jinn, go in peace; but if you are a man, wait a while, until dawn breaks and the day comes, and the night carries its darkness away.”
sentences.n: insī, “human”, the adjective of ins, mankind. labitha maliyyan, “to tarry a good while”; the print marks the doubled yāʾ of maliyyan. Rhyme: nahār, iʿtikār. iʿtikār, of the night, is its darkness thickening; dhahaba bi-, “to go off with, take away”: the night leaves and takes its murk with it.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ لَبِثَ الْمُنَادِي مَكَانَهُ وَلَبِثَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ مَكَانَهُ وَلَمْ يَزَالَا يَتَنَاشَدَانِ الْأَشْعَارَ وَيَبْكِيَانِ بِالدُّمُوعِ الْغِزَارِ حَتَّى طَلَعَ ضَوْءُ النَّهَارِ وَذَهَبَ اللَّيْلُ بِالِاعْتِكَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma labitha al-munādī makānahu wa-labitha kāna mā kāna makānahu wa-lam yazālā yatanāshadāni al-ashʿāra wa-yabkiyāni bi-al-dumūʿi al-ghizāri ḥattā ṭalaʿa ḍawʾu al-nahāri wa-dhahaba al-laylu bi-al-iʿtikāri
sentences.l: Then the caller stayed (in) his place, and Kān Mā Kān stayed (in) his place, and they did not cease reciting-to-each-other the poems and weeping with the tears abundant, until the light of the day rose and the night went with the darkness.
sentences.i: So the caller stayed where he was, and Kān Mā Kān stayed where he was, and the two of them went on reciting verses to each other and shedding copious tears until daylight came and the night carried its darkness away.
sentences.n: tanāshada, “to recite verses to one another”, the reciprocal form of anshada. lam yazālā, “they did not cease”, with a following verb: “they kept on”. ghizār, plural of ghazīr, “abundant”. Rhyme: ashʿār, ghizār, nahār, iʿtikār.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ إِلَيْهِ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَوَجَدَهُ رَجُلًا مِنْ عَرَبِ الْبَادِيَةِ إِلَّا أَنَّهُ شَابٌّ فِي سِنِّهِ وَعَلَيْهِ ثِيَابٌ رَثَّةٌ مُتَقَلِّدٌ بِسَيْفٍ صَدِىٌ فِى جَفِيرِهِ وَآثَارُ الْعِشْقِ عَلَيْهِ لَائِحَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara ilayhi kāna mā kāna fa-wajadahu rajulan min ʿarabi al-bādiyati illā annahu shābbun fī sinnihi wa-ʿalayhi thiyābun raththatun mutaqalladun bi-sayfin ṣadiyun fī jafīrihi wa-āthāru al-ʿishqi ʿalayhi lāʾiḥatun
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān looked at him, and he found him a man of the Arabs of the desert, except that he was a youth in his age, and on him were clothes threadbare; girded with a sword rusty in its scabbard; and the traces of passion upon him were showing.
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān looked at him, and found that it was one of the desert Arabs, but a young man in years, dressed in threadbare clothes, a sword gone rusty in its sheath slung at his side, and the marks of love plain upon him.
sentences.n: bādiya, “open desert”: ʿarab al-bādiya are the Bedouin. shābb fī sinnihi, “young in his age”. mutaqalladun, “girded”, is pointed here as a further predicate (“he was girded”); Classical style would put it in the accusative as a circumstantial word, mutaqalladan, with an alif the print does not write. taqallada bi-sayf, “to hang a sword on oneself”, by its baldric over the shoulder (qilāda, “neck-band”). The print points ṣadiyun, “rusty”, in the nominative with tanwīn, though it describes sayfin and agreement would want the genitive ṣadiʾin; the marks are kept as printed. jafīr is properly a quiver for arrows; here it serves for the sword's sheath. lāʾiḥ, “appearing, showing plainly”.

sentences.t: فَأَتَى إِلَيْهِ وَتَقَدَّمَ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ الْبَدَوِيُّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامَ وَحَيَّاهُ بِالْإِكْرَامِ إِلَّا أَنَّهُ احْتَقَرَهُ لِمَا رَأَى مِنْ صِغَرِ سِنِّهِ وَحَالَتُهُ حَالَةُ فَقِيرٍ
sentences.tr: fa-atā ilayhi wa-taqaddama wa-sallama ʿalayhi fa-radda al-badawiyyu ʿalayhi al-salāma wa-ḥayyāhu bi-al-ikrāmi illā annahu iḥtaqarahu li-mā raʾā min ṣighari sinnihi wa-ḥālatuhu ḥālatu faqīrin
sentences.l: So he came to him, and stepped forward and greeted him; and the Bedouin returned the greeting to him and saluted him with the honouring, except that he despised him for what he saw of the smallness of his age, his state being the state of a poor-man.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān went up to him, stepped forward and greeted him. The Bedouin returned his greeting and welcomed him courteously, but he looked down on him, seeing how young he was, and that he had all the look of a pauper.
sentences.n: The print marks the doubled letters of taqaddama, sallama, radda, ḥayyāhu and illā. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”: the greeting is al-salāmu ʿalaykum, and radda ʿalayhi al-salām is to answer it. ḥayyā, “to greet, wish long life to”. li-mā raʾā min, “for what he saw of”: li- gives the reason. wa-ḥālatuhu ḥālatu faqīrin, “and his state the state of a poor man”: a circumstantial clause brought in by wa-.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ يَافَتَى مِنْ أَيِّ الْقَوْمِ أَنْتَ وَإِلَى مَنْ تُنْسَبُ مِنَ الْعُرْبَانِ وَمَا قِصَّتُكَ وَأَنْتَ سَائِرٌ فِى اللَّيْلِ وَهُوَ فِعْلُ الْأَبْطَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu yā fatā min ayyi al-qawmi anta wa-ilā man tunsabu mina al-ʿurbāni wa-mā qiṣṣatuka wa-anta sāʾirun fī al-layli wa-huwa fiʿlu al-abṭāli
sentences.l: And he said to him: O young-man, of which of the people are you, and to whom are you traced-in-lineage of the Arabs, and what is your story, while you are travelling in the night, and it is the doing of the heroes?
sentences.i: “Young man,” he said, “what people are you from, and to which of the tribes do you trace your descent? And what is your story, travelling by night as you are, which is a thing only heroes do?
sentences.n: The print runs yā into fatā (يافتى) and marks the doubled yāʾ of ayyi and the ṣād of qiṣṣatuka. nusiba ilā, “to be traced in lineage to”: the Bedouin's first question to a stranger is always his tribe. ʿurbān, a later plural of ʿarab, “Bedouin Arabs”, common in the Nights. sāʾir, “going, travelling”, from sāra.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ كَلَّمْتَنِي فِى اللَّيْلِ كَلَامًا لَا يَتَكَلَّمُ بِهِ إِلَّا كُلُّ فَارِسٍ هُمَامٍ وَبَطَلٍ ضِرْغَامٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qad kallamtanī fī al-layli kalāman lā yatakallamu bihi illā kullu fārisin humāmin wa-baṭalin ḍirghāmin
sentences.l: And you have spoken-to-me in the night speech that none speaks it except every horseman high-minded and hero lion-like.
sentences.i: You spoke to me in the night in words that only a gallant horseman or a lion-hearted hero would use.
sentences.n: The print marks the tāʾ of kallamtanī with fatḥa: “you spoke to me”, addressed to a man. Rhymed prose: abṭāl above, then humām, ḍirghām. humām, “high-minded, valiant”, is a hero's epithet; ḍirghām, “lion”, used here as an adjective, “lion-like”. The words he means are Kān Mā Kān's challenge and verses in the dark, just before.

sentences.t: وَالْآنَ رُوحُكَ فِي قَبْضَتِي وَلٰكِنِّي أَرْحَمُكَ لِصِغَرِ سِنِّكَ فَأَجْعَلُكَ رَفِيقِي وَتَكُونُ عِنْدِي بِرَسْمِ خِدْمَتِي
sentences.tr: wa-al-āna rūḥuka fī qabḍatī wa-lākinnī arḥamuka li-ṣighari sinnika fa-ajʿaluka rafīqī wa-takūnu ʿindī bi-rasmi khidmatī
sentences.l: And now your soul is in my grasp; but I take-pity-on you for the smallness of your age, so I will make you my companion, and you shall be with me by appointment of my service.
sentences.i: Now your life is in my hand. But I pity you for your youth, so I will make you my companion, and you shall stay with me as my servant.”
sentences.n: qabḍa, “grip, grasp”: what the hand closes on. Rhyme: qabḍatī, khidmatī. bi-rasmi, “by appointment of, for the purpose of”, is a later, chancery-style idiom: rasm is an official order or allotment, and bi-rasmi khidmatī means “assigned to my service”. Note how quickly “companion” slides into “servant”: that is what Kān Mā Kān hears.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَظَاعَةَ كَلَامِهِ بَعْدَ مَا أَبْدَاهُ مِنْ حُسْنِ نِظَامِهِ عَلِمَ أَنَّهُ احْتَقَرَهُ وَطَمِعَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kāna mā kāna faẓāʿata kalāmihi baʿda mā abdāhu min ḥusni niẓāmihi ʿalima annahu iḥtaqarahu wa-ṭamiʿa fīhi
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān heard the ugliness of his speech, after what he had shown of the beauty of his arranging, he knew that he despised him and coveted him.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān heard how coarse his words were, after the fine verses he had let him hear, he knew that the Bedouin despised him and had designs on him.
sentences.n: Rhyme: kalāmihi, niẓāmihi. faẓāʿa, “ugliness, harshness”. niẓām, “arrangement”, especially the stringing of verse, as niẓām is the thread that strings pearls: the Bedouin had been reciting poetry. ṭamiʿa fī, “to covet, to set one's greed on”: he meant to make Kān Mā Kān his servant.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ بِكَلَامٍ لَيِّنٍ فَصِيحٍ يَا وَجْهَ الْعَرَبِ دَعْنَا مِنْ صِغَرِ سِنِّي وَأَخْبِرْنِي عَنْ سَبَبِ سَيْرِكَ بِاللَّيْلِ فِى الْقِفَارِ وَإِنْشَادِكَ الْأَشْعَارَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu bi-kalāmin layyinin faṣīḥin yā wajha al-ʿarabi daʿnā min ṣighari sinnī wa-akhbirnī ʿan sababi sayrika bi-al-layli fī al-qifāri wa-inshādika al-ashʿāra
sentences.l: And he said to him in speech soft, eloquent: O face of the Arabs, leave us from the smallness of my age, and tell me of the cause of your going by night in the wastes, and your reciting the poems.
sentences.i: So he answered him in gentle, well-turned words: “Chief of the Arabs, let my youth be. Tell me rather why you travel by night through the wilderness reciting verses.
sentences.n: The print marks the doubled yāʾ of layyin, “soft, gentle”. faṣīḥ, “eloquent, of pure speech”. wajh al-ʿarab, “face of the Arabs”: a courteous address, “O foremost of the Arabs”, wajh being the notable, the man of standing. daʿnā min, “leave us from”, “never mind”. Rhyme: qifār, ashʿār.

sentences.t: وَأَرَاكَ تَذْكُرُأَنَّنِي أَخْدُمُكَ فَمَنْ تَكُونُ أَنْتَ وَمَا حَمَلَكَ عَلَى هٰذَا الْمَقَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-arāka tadhkuru annanī akhdumuka fa-man takūnu anta wa-mā ḥamalaka ʿalā hādhā al-maqāli
sentences.l: And I see you mention that I shall serve you; so who may you be, and what has carried you onto this saying?
sentences.i: And I hear you say that I am to serve you. Who are you, then, and what has led you to talk like this?”
sentences.n: The print runs tadhkuru into annanī (تذكرانني). man takūnu anta, “who might you be?”: takūnu, “are”, is the everyday way of asking a stranger's identity. ḥamalahu ʿalā, “to carry someone onto”, to induce him to. maqāl, “saying, talk”, rhymes back to abṭāl, the Bedouin's own word.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ اسْمَعْ يَا غُلَامُ أَنَا صَبَّاحُ ابْنُ رَمَّاحِ بْنِ هَمَّامٍ وَقَوْمِي مِنْ عَرَبِ الشَّامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu ismaʿ yā ghulāmu anā ṣabbāḥu ibnu rammāḥi bni hammāmin wa-qawmī min ʿarabi al-shāmi
sentences.l: And he said to him: Listen, O boy: I am Ṣabbāḥ son of Rammāḥ son of Hammām, and my people are of the Arabs of al-Shām.
sentences.i: “Listen, boy,” said he. “I am Ṣabbāḥ ibn Rammāḥ ibn Hammām, and my people are Bedouin of Syria.
sentences.n: ghulām, “boy, lad”, also “servant”: he keeps Kān Mā Kān in his place. The print writes the first ibn with its alif and the second without (ابن … بن). The names are all intensive forms and suit a raider: rammāḥ, “spearman”; ṣabbāḥ, perhaps “one who attacks at dawn” (ṣabāḥ, morning, is the hour of the raid); hammām, “one of great resolve”. Rhyme: hammām, shām. al-Shām is Syria, the land north of Arabia.

sentences.t: وَلِي بِنْتُ عَمٍّ اسْمُهَا نَجْمَهُ كُلُّ مَنْ رَآهَا أَتَتْهُ النِّعْمَةُ
sentences.tr: wa-lī bintu ʿammin ismuhā najmatu kullu man raʾāhā atathu al-niʿmatu
sentences.l: And I have a daughter of an uncle whose name is Najma; every one who saw her, the blessing came to him.
sentences.i: I have a cousin named Najma, and whoever sets eyes on her is blessed.
sentences.n: bint ʿamm, “daughter of a paternal uncle”: among the Bedouin she is the cousin a young man has the first claim to marry. Najma means “star”. The print spells her name with a plain hāʾ (نجمه), and so in the next sentence, beside niʿma written with tāʾ marbūṭa; the two rhyme (najma, niʿma). kullu man … atathu, “everyone who … came to him”: the subject is set at the head and taken up again by the pronoun.

sentences.t: وَمَاتَ وَالِدِي وَتَرَبَّيْتُ عِنْدَ عَمِّي أَبِي نَجْمَهَ
sentences.tr: wa-māta wālidī wa-tarabbaytu ʿinda ʿammī abī najmata
sentences.l: And my father died, and I was raised with my uncle, the father of Najma.
sentences.i: My father died and I was brought up in the house of my uncle, Najma's father.
sentences.n: The print marks the doubled bāʾ of tarabbaytu, “I was brought up”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَبِرْتُ أَنَا وَكَبِرَتْ بِنْتُ عَمِّي حَجَبَهَا عَنِّي وَحَجَبَنِي عَنْهَا لَمَّا رَآنِي فَقِيرَ الْحَالِ قَلِيلَ الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kabirtu anā wa-kabirat bintu ʿammī ḥajabahā ʿannī wa-ḥajabanī ʿanhā lammā raʾānī faqīra al-ḥāli qalīla al-māli
sentences.l: And when I grew-up, I, and my uncle's daughter grew-up, he veiled her from me and veiled me from her, when he saw me poor of the state, little of the wealth.
sentences.i: When I grew up, and my cousin grew up too, he kept her from me and me from her, seeing that I was poor, with little to my name.
sentences.n: The same thing has just happened to Kān Mā Kān and Qaḍā Fakān in Baghdad: the two young men's stories mirror each other. ḥajaba, “to screen, keep out of sight”. Rhyme: ḥāl, māl. faqīr al-ḥāl, qalīl al-māl, “poor of condition, little of wealth”: adjectives in construct with the noun they describe.

sentences.t: فَدَخَّلْتُ الْعَرَبَ الْكِبَارَ وَسَادَاتِ الْقَبَائِلِ وَسُقْتُ عَلَيْهِ فَاسْتَحَى مِنْهُمْ وَأَجَابَ أَنْ يُعْطِيَنِي بِنْتَ عَمِّي
sentences.tr: fa-dakhkhaltu al-ʿaraba al-kibāra wa-sādāti al-qabāʾili wa-suqtu ʿalayhi fa-istaḥā minhum wa-ajāba an yuʿṭiyanī binta ʿammī
sentences.l: So I brought-in the great Arabs and the lords of the tribes, and drove them upon him; and he was ashamed before them, and consented that he give me my uncle's daughter.
sentences.i: So I brought in the great men of the Arabs and the chiefs of the tribes to plead with him, and he was ashamed to refuse them, and agreed to give me my cousin.
sentences.n: dakhkhaltu, “I brought in”, is read as a colloquial Form II with the sense of Classical adkhaltu: he made the elders go in to his uncle as intercessors. sāqa ʿalā, “to drive upon”, is in later and colloquial Arabic to urge someone by sending intercessors, to entreat him in the name of others. istaḥā, “to be ashamed”, the short form of istaḥyā. ajāba an, “to consent to”.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنَّهُ اشْتَرَطَ عَلَيَّ فِي مَهْرِهَا خَمْسِينَ رَأْسًا مِنَ الْخَيْلِ وَخَمْسِينَ نَاقَةً عِشَارِيَّاتٍ وَخَمْسِينَ جَمَلًا مُحَمَّلَةَ بُرٍّ وَمِثْلُهَا شَعِيرٌ وَعَشَرَةَ عَبِيدٍ وَعَشْرَ جَوَارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lākinnahu ishtaraṭa ʿalayya fī mahrihā khamsīna raʾsan mina al-khayli wa-khamsīna nāqatan ʿishāriyyātin wa-khamsīna jamalan muḥammalata burrin wa-mithluhā shaʿīrun wa-ʿasharata ʿabīdin wa-ʿashra jawārin
sentences.l: But he laid-as-condition on me for her bride-price fifty head of the horses, and fifty she-camels ten-months-pregnant, and fifty camels laden of wheat, and the like of them barley, and ten slaves and ten slave-girls.
sentences.i: But he made it a condition that for her bride-price I should bring him fifty head of horses, fifty she-camels heavy with young, fifty camels laden with wheat and as many with barley, ten male slaves and ten slave-girls.
sentences.n: mahr, the bride-price the groom pays. The print marks the shadda of ʿalayya and of burr, “wheat”. ʿishāriyyāt is from ʿishār, she-camels in the tenth month of pregnancy, the most prized of a herd; the print's ʿishāriyyāt is a later adjective formed from that plural. muḥammalata burrin, “laden with wheat”, is read as an adjective in construct with what it carries, since the print does not write the accusative alif of burran. In the same way wa-mithluhā shaʿīrun, “and the like of them, barley”, is pointed as it stands, where Classical style would want shaʿīran; and jawārin, “slave-girls”, keeps the short form where the accusative would be jawāriya. Spoken Arabic had long dropped these endings.

sentences.t: وَحَمَّلَنِي مَا لَا أُطِيقُ وَأَكْثَرَ عَلَيَّ فِى الصَّدَاقِ وَهَا أَنَا مُسَافِرٌ مِنَ الشَّامِ إِلَى الْعِرَاقِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥammalanī mā lā uṭīqu wa-akthara ʿalayya fī al-ṣadāqi wa-hā anā musāfirun mina al-shāmi ilā al-ʿirāqi
sentences.l: And he loaded me with what I cannot bear, and made-much against me in the dowry; and here I am travelling from al-Shām to al-ʿIrāq.
sentences.i: He laid on me more than I can bear and set the marriage gift too high for me; and so here I am, on my way from Syria to Iraq.
sentences.n: Rhyme: uṭīq, ṣadāq, ʿirāq. ṣadāq is another word for the bride-price, mahr. akthara ʿalā, “to make it too much for”. The print marks the shadda of ʿalayya. hā anā, “here I am”.

sentences.t: وَلِي عِشْرُونَ يَوْمًا مَا نَظَرْتُ أَحَدًا سِوَاكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lī ʿishrūna yawman mā naẓartu aḥadan siwāka
sentences.l: And I have twenty days, I have not seen anyone other than you.
sentences.i: For twenty days I have seen no one but you.
sentences.n: wa-lī ʿishrūna yawman, “and to me are twenty days”: the usual way to say how long one has been doing something.

sentences.t: وَعَزَمْتُ أَنِّي أَدْخُلُ بَغْدَادَ وَأَنْظُرُ مَنْ يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا مِنَ التُّجَّارِ الْمَيَاسِيرِ الْكِبَارِ فَأَخْرُجُ فِي أَثَرِهِمْ وَأُغِيرُ عَلَى أَمْوَالِهِمْ وَأَقْتُلُ رِجَالَهُمْ وَأَسُوقُ جِمَالَهُمْ وَأَحْمَالَهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿazamtu annī adkhulu baghdāda wa-anẓuru man yakhruju minhā mina al-tujjāri al-mayāsīri al-kibāri fa-akhruju fī atharihim wa-ughīru ʿalā amwālihim wa-aqtulu rijālahum wa-asūqu jimālahum wa-aḥmālahum
sentences.l: And I resolved that I go-in to Baghdad and watch who goes out from it of the merchants, the rich-ones, the great-ones; then I go out on their track, and raid upon their goods, and kill their men, and drive-off their camels and their loads.
sentences.i: I have made up my mind to go to Baghdad and watch for rich and important merchants leaving the city; then I shall follow on their track, fall upon their goods, kill their men and drive off their camels and their loads.
sentences.n: ʿazamtu annī adkhulu, “I resolved that I enter”: Classical style says ʿazamtu ʿalā an adkhula; the text uses annī with the plain present, a later construction. mayāsīr, plural of maysūr, “well-off, wealthy”. Rhyme: tujjār, mayāsīr, kibār; then amwālihim, rijālahum, jimālahum, aḥmālahum. aghāra ʿalā, “to raid”: the ghazw of the desert, here turned on Baghdad's caravans.

sentences.t: فَمَنْ تَكُونُ أَنْتَ مِنَ النَّاسِ
sentences.tr: fa-man takūnu anta mina al-nāsi
sentences.l: So who may you be, of the people?
sentences.i: So who might you be?
sentences.n: He turns Kān Mā Kān's own question back on him (fa-man takūnu anta).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِنَّ قِصَّتَكَ مِثْلُ قِصَّتِي غَيْرَ أَنَّ مَرَضِي أَخْطَرُ مِنْ مَرَضِكَ لِأَنَّ ابْنَةَ عَمِّي بِنْتُ مَلِكٍ وَأَهْلُهَا لَا يَكْفِيهِمْ مِنِّي مَا ذَكَرْتَ وَلَا يُرْضِيهِمْ شَيْءٌ مِثْلُ هٰذَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla kāna mā kāna inna qiṣṣataka mithlu qiṣṣatī ghayra anna maraḍī akhṭaru min maraḍika li-anna ibnata ʿammī bintu malikin wa-ahluhā lā yakfīhim minnī mā dhakarta wa-lā yurḍīhim shayʾun mithlu hādhā
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said: Truly your story is like my story, except that my sickness is more-dangerous than your sickness, because the daughter of my uncle is the daughter of a king, and her people, there would not suffice them from me what you mentioned, nor would satisfy them a thing like this.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān said, “Your story is just like mine, except that my sickness is graver than yours: my cousin is a king's daughter, and her family would not be content to have from me what you have named, nor would anything of the sort satisfy them.”
sentences.n: maraḍ, “sickness”: love as an illness, a commonplace. mā dhakarta, “what you mentioned”, is the bride-price the Bedouin has just listed; the print marks the final vowel of dhakarta, “you mentioned”. Qaḍā Fakān is indeed a king's daughter: her father was King Sharrukān. kafā, “to be enough for”, takes its object directly (yakfīhim), and min marks what is had from him.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ صَبَّاحٌ لَعَلَّكَ مَهْبُولٌ أَوْ مِنْ كَثْرَةِ الْعِشْقِ مَخْبُولٌ كَيْفَ تَكُونُ بِنْتُ عَمِّكَ بِنْتَ مَلِكٍ وَأَنْتَ مَا عَلَيْكَ سِيمَةُ الْمُلُوكِ وَمَا أَنْتَ إِلَّا صُعْلُوكٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ṣabbāḥun laʿallaka mahbūlun aw min kathrati al-ʿishqi makhbūlun kayfa takūnu bintu ʿammika binta malikin wa-anta mā ʿalayka sīmatu al-mulūki wa-mā anta illā ṣuʿlūkun
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ said: Perhaps you are crazed, or from the muchness of the passion deranged. How is the daughter of your uncle the daughter of a king, when you, there is not on you the mark of the kings, and you are not but a pauper?
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ said, “You must be mad, or else crazed with too much love! How can your cousin be a king's daughter, when there is nothing of the king about you, and you are nothing but a beggar?”
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: mahbūl, makhbūl; mulūk, ṣuʿlūk. mahbūl, “crazy, simple”, is a word of the spoken language; makhbūl, “deranged, out of his wits”, is its Classical neighbour, and the pair chime in sound as well as sense. The print marks the doubled lām of laʿallaka. sīma, “mark, distinguishing sign”. ṣuʿlūk, “pauper, vagabond”, the word used of the poor folk among whom he and his mother went to live.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا وَجْهَ الْعَرَبِ لَا تَسْتَغْرِبْ هٰذَا الْحَالَ وَمَا فَاتَ فَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā wajha al-ʿarabi lā tastaghrib hādhā al-ḥāla wa-mā fāta fāta
sentences.l: And he said: O face of the Arabs, do not find-strange this state; and what has passed has passed.
sentences.i: He said, “O noblest of the Arabs, do not wonder at my condition: what is gone is gone.
sentences.n: yā wajha al-ʿarab, “O face of the Arabs”, is a courteous address to a Bedouin: wajh, “face”, also means the foremost, the honour of a people. istaghraba, “to find strange”. ḥāl, “state”, is often feminine, but here it takes the masculine hādhā. mā fāta fāta, “what has passed has passed”: a proverbial shrug.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ شِئْتَ مِنِّي الْبَيَانَ فَأَنَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ بْنُ الْمَلِكِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ ابْنِ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ صَاحِبِ بَغْدَادَ وَأَرْضِ خُرَاسَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-in shiʾta minnī al-bayāna fa-anā kāna mā kāna bnu al-maliki ḍawʾi al-makāni ibni al-maliki ʿumara bni al-nuʿmāni ṣāḥibi baghdāda wa-arḍi khurāsāna
sentences.l: And if you wish from me the clear-account: I am Kān Mā Kān, son of the king Ḍawʾ al-Makān, son of the king ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, lord of Baghdad and the land of Khurāsān.
sentences.i: But if you want the plain truth from me, I am Kān Mā Kān, son of King Ḍawʾ al-Makān, son of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, lord of Baghdad and the land of Khurāsān.
sentences.n: From here to the end of his speech Kān Mā Kān talks in rhymed prose on -ān: bayān, makān, nuʿmān, khurāsān, and on through zamān, sāsān, insān. bayān, “clear statement, explanation”. The print writes bn without its alif after the hero's name, as usual between a name and the father's name, but ibn in full before al-malik ʿUmar. ṣāḥib, “owner, lord”, agrees with ʿUmar.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ جَارَ عَلَيَّ الزَّمَانُ فَمَاتَ وَالِدِي وَتَسَلْطَنَ الْمَلِكُ سَاسَانُ وَخَرَجْتُ مِنْ بَغْدَادَ خِفْيَةً لِئَلَّا يَرَانِي إِنْسَانٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qad jāra ʿalayya al-zamānu fa-māta wālidī wa-tasalṭana al-maliku sāsānu wa-kharajtu min baghdāda khifyatan li-allā yarānī insānun
sentences.l: And time has wronged me: my father died, and al-Malik Sāsān became-sultan, and I went out from Baghdad in secret, lest a human see me.
sentences.i: Fortune has dealt unjustly with me: my father died, al-Malik Sāsān made himself sultan, and I have left Baghdad in secret, so that no one should see me.
sentences.n: jāra ʿalā, “to deal unjustly with”: ʿalā marks the one wronged; the print marks the doubled yāʾ of ʿalayya. tasalṭana, “to become sultan”, a verb made from sulṭān, of later Arabic. khifyatan, “secretly”. li-allā, “lest”, which the print spells with its hamza (لئلا).

sentences.t: فَهَا أَنَا قَدْ أَوْضَحْتُ لَكَ الْبَيَانَ وَلِي عِشْرُونَ يَوْمًا مَا رَأَيْتُ أَحَدًا غَيْرَكَ فَقِصَّتُكَ مِثْلُ قِصَّتِي وَحَاجَتُكَ مِثْلُ حَاجَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-hā anā qad awḍaḥtu laka al-bayāna wa-lī ʿishrūna yawman mā raʾaytu aḥadan ghayraka fa-qiṣṣatuka mithlu qiṣṣatī wa-ḥājatuka mithlu ḥājatī
sentences.l: So here I am: I have made-clear to you the account. And to me are twenty days I have not seen anyone other than you; so your story is like my story, and your need is like my need.
sentences.i: There, I have made it all plain to you. For twenty days I have seen no one but you. Your story is like mine, and your need is like mine.”
sentences.n: wa-lī ʿishrūna yawman, “and I have had twenty days”, the spoken way of saying “for twenty days now”: he echoes the Bedouin's own words, who also had seen no one for twenty days. awḍaḥa al-bayān, “to make the explanation clear”, a pleonasm for the rhyme.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ ذٰلِكَ صَبَّاحٌ صَاحَ وَافَرْحَتِي فَإِنِّي بَلَغْتُ مُنْيَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa dhālika ṣabbāḥun ṣāḥa wā-farḥatī fa-innī balaghtu munyatī
sentences.l: And when Ṣabbāḥ heard that, he cried out: O my joy! For I have reached my wish.
sentences.i: When Ṣabbāḥ heard this he cried out, “Oh, joy! I have got my wish!
sentences.n: ṣabbāḥ … ṣāḥa, “Ṣabbāḥ … cried out”: the name and the verb make a jingle. wā-farḥatī, “O my joy!”: wā- is the particle of lament (wā-ḥasratāh, “alas!”), turned here to a shout of delight, a common jest of the spoken language. munya, “wish, desire”. Rhyme: farḥatī, munyatī.

sentences.t: وَلَيْسَ لِي الْيَوْمَ كَسْبٌ غَيْرُكَ لِأَنَّكَ مِنْ ذُرِّيَّةِ الْمُلُوكِ وَخَرَجْتَ فِي زِيِّ صُعْلُوكٍ وَلَا بُدَّ أَنَّ أَهْلَكَ يَطْلُبُونَكَ وَإِذَا وَجَدُوكَ عِنْدَ أَحَدٍ فَبِالْأَمْوَالِ الْجَزِيلَةِ يَفْدُونَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-laysa lī al-yawma kasbun ghayruka li-annaka min dhurriyyati al-mulūki wa-kharajta fī ziyyi ṣuʿlūkin wa-lā budda anna ahlaka yaṭlubūnaka wa-idhā wajadūka ʿinda aḥadin fa-bi-al-amwāli al-jazīlati yafdūnaka
sentences.l: And there is not for me today a gain other than you, because you are of the offspring of the kings and went out in the garb of a pauper; and no escape that your people are seeking you, and when they find you with someone, then with wealth abundant they ransom you.
sentences.i: Today you are all the booty I need. You are of the seed of kings, though you have come out dressed as a beggar; your family is sure to be looking for you, and when they find you in someone's hands they will ransom you for a great sum of money.
sentences.n: kasb, “gain, earnings”: the would-be raider has found his prize. More rhyme: mulūk, ṣuʿlūk; yaṭlubūnaka, yafdūnaka. The print marks the doubled yāʾ of ziyy, “dress, garb”, and the doubled nūn of anna. lā budda anna, “there is no escape (from the fact) that”: certainly. fadā, “to ransom”; bi- marks the price, and is put first for emphasis.

sentences.t: هَيَّا فَاَدِرْ كِتَافَكَ يَا غُلَامِي وَامْشِ قُدَّ امِي
sentences.tr: hayyā fa-adir kitāfaka yā ghulāmī wa-imshi quddāmī
sentences.l: Come on, then turn your shoulders, O my slave-boy, and walk in-front-of-me.
sentences.i: Come, my lad, put your arms behind your back, and walk on ahead of me.”
sentences.n: hayyā, “come on!”; the print marks its doubled yāʾ. adir kitāfaka, “turn your shoulders”: kitāf, a plural of katif, “shoulder”, and also the word for the cord that pinions a captive's arms behind his back; he is told to put his arms back to be bound. The print points adir, “turn”, imperative of adāra. ghulām, “boy, servant, slave-boy”: he is already counting him his property. The print splits quddāmī, “in front of me”, into two words (قد امي); quddām is the everyday word, Classical quddāma.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ لَا تَفْعَلْ يَا أَخَا الْعَرَبِ لِأَنَّ أَهْلِي لَا يَشْتَرُونَنِي بِفِضَّةٍ وَلَا ذَهَبٍ وَلَا بِدِرْهَمِ نُحَاسٍ وَأَنَا رَجُلٌ فَقِيرٌ وَلَا مَعِي قَلِيلٌ وَلَا كَثِيرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla kāna mā kāna lā tafʿal yā akhā al-ʿarabi li-anna ahlī lā yashtarūnanī bi-fiḍḍatin wa-lā dhahabin wa-lā bi-dirhami nuḥāsin wa-anā rajulun faqīrun wa-lā maʿī qalīlun wa-lā kathīrun
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said: Do not do (it), O brother of the Arabs, because my people will not buy me with silver nor gold nor with a dirham of copper; and I am a poor man, and not with me (is) little nor much.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān said, “Do not do it, brother Arab. My people would not buy me back for silver or gold, no, not for a copper coin. I am a poor man, and I have nothing with me, little or much.
sentences.n: The print has بفصة, a misprint for بفضة, bi-fiḍḍatin, “for silver”, corrected here. yā akhā al-ʿarab, “O brother of the Arabs”, a friendly way of addressing a Bedouin. ishtarā bi-, “to buy for”: bi- marks the price. A dirham was properly a silver coin; dirham nuḥās, “a copper dirham”, is the smallest of small change.

sentences.t: فَدَعْ عَنْكَ هٰذِهِ الْأَخْلَاقَ وَاتَّخِذْنِي مِنَ الرِّفَاقِ وَاخْرُجْ بِنَا مِنْ أَرْضِ الْعِرَاقِ لِنَجُولَ فِي نَوَاحِي الْآفَاقِ لَعَلَّنَا نَظْفَرُ بِالْمَهْرِ وَالصَّدَاقِ وَنَحْظَى مِنْ بَنَاتِ عَمِّنَا بِالتَّقْبِيلِ وَالْعِنَاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-daʿ ʿanka hādhihi al-akhlāqa wa-ittakhidhnī mina al-rifāqi wa-ukhruj binā min arḍi al-ʿirāqi li-najūla fī nawāḥī al-āfāqi laʿallanā naẓfaru bi-al-mahri wa-al-ṣadāqi wa-naḥẓā min banāti ʿamminā bi-al-taqbīli wa-al-ʿināqi
sentences.l: So leave from you these manners, and take me among the companions, and go out with us from the land of al-ʿIrāq, that we may roam in the regions of the horizons; perhaps we may win the bride-price and the dowry, and we may be-favoured from the daughters of our uncle with the kissing and the embracing.
sentences.i: Give up these ways of yours: take me for your comrade, and let us leave the land of Iraq and roam the far corners of the world. Perhaps we shall come by the bride-price and the dowry, and win kisses and embraces from our cousins.”
sentences.n: Rhymed prose all on -āq: akhlāq, rifāq, ʿirāq, āfāq, ṣadāq, ʿināq. daʿ ʿanka, “leave off, put from you”. akhlāq, “manners, ways of behaving”. ittakhadha … min, “to take as one of”; the print marks the doubled tāʾ of ittakhidhnī and the doubled mīm of ʿamminā. āfāq, plural of ufuq, “horizon”: the ends of the earth. mahr and ṣadāq are both words for the marriage gift a groom pays; the pair is for the rhyme. ḥaẓiya bi-, “to obtain as a favour, enjoy”: bi- marks what is won, min the one it comes from. banāt ʿamminā, “the daughters of our uncle”, each man's own cousin.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ صَبَّاحٌ ذٰلِكَ الْكَلَامَ غَضِبَ وَزَادَ بِهِ الْإِعْجَابُ وَالِالْتِهَابُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ṣabbāḥun dhālika al-kalāma ghaḍiba wa-zāda bihi al-iʿjābu wa-al-iltihābu
sentences.l: And when Ṣabbāḥ heard that speech he grew-angry, and there increased in him the self-conceit and the inflaming.
sentences.i: When Ṣabbāḥ heard this he flew into a rage, his pride swelling and his temper blazing.
sentences.n: iʿjāb, “admiration”, and especially self-admiration, conceit (uʿjiba bi-nafsihi, “he was pleased with himself”); iltihāb, “flaring up, blazing”, of fire or of anger. zāda bihi, “increased in him”: bi- marks the one in whom it grows. The rhyme in -āb runs on through the next sentence.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ اَتُرَادِدُنِي فِى الْجَوَابِ يَا أَخَسَّ الْكِلَابِ اَدِرْ كِتَافَكَ وَإِلَّا أَنْزَلْتُ عَلَيْكَ الْعَذَابَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu waylaka a-turādidunī fī al-jawābi yā akhassa al-kilābi adir kitāfaka wa-illā anzaltu ʿalayka al-ʿadhāba
sentences.l: And he said to him: Woe to you! Do you bandy-words with me in the answer, O vilest of the dogs? Turn your shoulders, or else I have brought down on you the torment.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Damn you! Do you answer me back, you vilest of dogs? Put your arms behind you, or I will bring down punishment on you.”
sentences.n: Rhyme: jawāb, kilāb, ʿadhāb. waylaka, “woe to you!”, an accusative of imprecation. a-turādidunī, “do you bandy words with me?”, with the question particle a-, which the print points, as it points adir; rādada, “to answer back, argue”, is left here with its two dāls apart, where Classical would run them together (turāddunī). akhass, “vilest”, the print marking its doubled sīn. wa-illā, “or else”, followed by a perfect, anzaltu, “I have brought down”: the threat is spoken as though already carried out. The print writes fī with a dotless yāʾ (فى), here and below.

sentences.t: فَتَبَسَّمَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ كَيْفَ أُدِيرُ لَكَ الْكِتَافَ أَمَا عِنْدَكَ إِنْصَافٌ
sentences.tr: fa-tabassama kāna mā kāna wa-qāla lahu kayfa udīru laka al-kitāfa amā ʿindaka inṣāfun
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān smiled and said to him: How shall I turn for you the shoulders? Is there not with you fairness?
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān smiled and said to him, “How can I put my arms behind me for you? Have you no sense of fair play?
sentences.n: kitāf, inṣāf: rhymed prose again. amā, “is there not …?”, a question expecting “yes”. inṣāf, “fairness, giving each his due”. The print marks the doubled sīn of tabassama.

sentences.t: أَمَا تَخْشَى مُعَايَرَةَ الْعُرْبَانِ أَنْ تَسُوقَ رَجُلًا مِثْلِي أَسِيرًا فِى الذُّلِّ وَالْهَوَانِ وَأَنْتَ مَا اخْتَبَرْتَهُ فِى الْمَيْدَانِ لِتَعْلَمَ هَلْ هُوَ فَارِسٌ أَوْ جَبَانٌ
sentences.tr: amā takhshā muʿāyarata al-ʿurbāni an tasūqa rajulan mithlī asīran fī al-dhulli wa-al-hawāni wa-anta mā ikhtabartahu fī al-maydāni li-taʿlama hal huwa fārisun aw jabānun
sentences.l: Do you not fear the reproaching of the Bedouins, that you drive a man like me, a captive, in the abasement and the contempt, and you have not tested him in the field, that you might know whether he is a horseman or a coward?
sentences.i: Are you not afraid the Bedouins will taunt you, for driving off a man like me as a captive, in shame and disgrace, without ever having tried him on the field to learn whether he is a knight or a coward?
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: ʿurbān, hawān, maydān, jabān. ʿurbān, “Bedouin Arabs”, a plural of ʿarab used for the desert tribes. muʿāyara, “reproaching one another, taunting”, from ʿār, “shame”. sāqa, “to drive (cattle or captives) before one”. al-dhull wa-al-hawān, “abasement and contempt”, a common pair. fāris, “horseman”, and so a warrior, a knight.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ صَبَّاحٌ وَقَالَ يَا لَلّٰهِ الْعَجَبُ إِنَّكَ فِي سِنِّ الْغُلَامِ وَلٰكِنَّكَ كَبِيرُ الْكَلَامِ لِأَنَّ هٰذَا الْقَوْلَ لَايَصْدُرُ إِلَّا عَنِ الْبَطَلِ الْمِصْدَامِ فَمَا تُرِيدُ مِنْ إِنْصَافٍ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika ṣabbāḥun wa-qāla yā la-llāhi al-ʿajabu innaka fī sinni al-ghulāmi wa-lākinnaka kabīru al-kalāmi li-anna hādhā al-qawla lā yaṣduru illā ʿani al-baṭali al-miṣdāmi fa-mā turīdu min inṣāfin
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ laughed and said: O for God, the wonder! Truly you are in the age of the boy, but you are big of the speech, because this saying does not issue except from the hero, the hard-charger. So what do you want of fairness?
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ laughed and said, “Good God, how strange! You are of a boy's years, but you talk big; for words like these come only from a hero who charges home. So what fair play is it you want?”
sentences.n: yā la-llāhi, “O God!”: the la- of appeal, which the print points; the full Classical cry of wonder is yā la-llāhi li-al-ʿajabi, “O God, for the wonder!”, and here al-ʿajab stands without its li-. Rhyme: ghulām, kalām, miṣdām. sinn, “age”; kabīr al-kalām, “big of speech”, a boaster or one who speaks above his years. The print runs lā into yaṣduru (لايصدر). ṣadara ʿan, “to issue from”. miṣdām, “one who charges hard, a doughty fighter”, from ṣadama, “to strike, collide”. The print marks the doubled lām of illā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِنْ كُنْتَ تُرِيدُنِي أَسِيرًا مَعَكَ وَفِي خِدْمَتِكَ فَارْمِ سِلَاحَكَ وَخَفِّفْ ثِيَابَكَ وَادْنُ مِنِّي وَصَارِعْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu kāna mā kāna in kunta turīdunī asīran maʿaka wa-fī khidmatika fa-irmi silāḥaka wa-khaffif thiyābaka wa-udnu minnī wa-ṣāriʿnī
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to him: If you are wanting me a captive with you and in your service, then throw down your weapons, and lighten your clothes, and come near to me and wrestle me.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān said to him, “If you want me as your captive and your servant, throw down your weapons, strip off your outer clothes, come close and wrestle with me.
sentences.n: irmi, “throw”, imperative of ramā, and udnu, “come near”, imperative of danā, both short-voweled because the weak final letter drops. khaffif thiyābaka, “lighten your clothes”: take off the heavy outer garments, as wrestlers do. ṣāraʿa, “to wrestle with”.

sentences.t: فَكُلُّ مَنْ صَرَعَ مِنَّا صَاحِبَهُ بَلَغَ مِنْهُ مَرَامَهُ وَجَعَلَهُ غُلَامَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-kullu man ṣaraʿa minnā ṣāḥibahu balagha minhu marāmahu wa-jaʿalahu ghulāmahu
sentences.l: So every one who throws, of us, his companion, he attains from him his aim and makes him his slave-boy.
sentences.i: Whichever of us throws the other shall have his will of him and make him his slave.”
sentences.n: ṣaraʿa, “to throw down, fell (in wrestling)”. marām, “aim, what one seeks”. Rhyme: marāmahu, ghulāmahu. The print marks the doubled nūn of minnā.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ صَبَّاحٌ وَقَالَ أَظُنُّ أَنَّ كَثْرَةَ كَلَامِكَ تَدُلُّ عَلَى قُرْبِ حِمَامِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika ṣabbāḥun wa-qāla aẓunnu anna kathrata kalāmika tadullu ʿalā qurbi ḥimāmika
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ laughed and said: I think that the muchness of your talk points to the nearness of your death.
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ laughed and said, “I think all this talk of yours shows that your end is near.”
sentences.n: Rhyme: kalāmika, ḥimāmika. ḥimām, “death, fated end”, is not ḥammām, “bath”; the print sets the same letters for both.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَهَضَ وَرَمَى سِلَاحَهُ وَشَمَّرَ أَذْيَالَهُ وَدَنَا مِنْ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَدَنَا مِنْهُ الْآخَرُ وَتَجَاذَبَا
sentences.tr: thumma nahaḍa wa-ramā silāḥahu wa-shammara adhyālahu wa-danā min kāna mā kāna fa-danā minhu al-ākharu wa-tajādhabā
sentences.l: Then he rose and threw down his weapons and tucked-up his skirts, and drew-near to Kān Mā Kān, and the other drew-near to him, and they pulled-at-each-other.
sentences.i: Then he got up, threw down his weapons, girded up his skirts and closed with Kān Mā Kān; the other closed with him, and they grappled.
sentences.n: shammara adhyālahu, “he tucked up his skirts”, the hem of the robe pulled into the belt to free the legs: the gesture of a man getting ready for hard work or a fight. tajādhaba, “to pull at one another”, form VI, the form of mutual action.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَهُ الْبَدَوِيُّ يَفُوقُ عَنْهُ وَيَرْجَحُ عَلَيْهِ كَمَا يَرْجَحُ الْقِنْطَارُ عَلَى الدِّينَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadahu al-badawiyyu yafūqu ʿanhu wa-yarjaḥu ʿalayhi ka-mā yarjaḥu al-qinṭāru ʿalā al-dīnāri
sentences.l: And the Bedouin found him surpassing over him and outweighing him, as the hundredweight outweighs the dinar.
sentences.i: And the Bedouin found him far stronger, outweighing him as a hundredweight outweighs a single dinar.
sentences.n: fāqa, “to surpass”, takes a direct object in Classical Arabic; yafūqu ʿanhu, with ʿan, is a looser turn of the text. rajaḥa ʿalā, “to outweigh”, is the language of the scales. qinṭār, a great weight (“hundredweight”); dīnār, a gold coin, a tiny one. Rhyme: qinṭār, dīnār.

sentences.t: وَنَظَرَ إِلَى ثَبَاتِ رِجْلَيْهِ فِى الْأَرْضِ فَوَجَدَهُمَا كَالْمَأْذَنَتَيْنِ الْمُؤَسَّسَتَيْنِ أَوْ وَتَدَيْنِ مَدْقُوقَيْنِ أَوْ جَبَلَيْنِ رَاسِخَيْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-naẓara ilā thabāti rijlayhi fī al-arḍi fa-wajadahumā ka-al-maʾdhanatayni al-muʾassasatayni aw watadayni madqūqayni aw jabalayni rāsikhayni
sentences.l: And he looked at the firmness of his two feet in the ground, and found them like the two minarets well-founded, or two tent-pegs driven-in, or two mountains firm-rooted.
sentences.i: He looked at how firmly Kān Mā Kān's feet were planted in the ground, and found them like two minarets set on deep foundations, or two tent-pegs driven home, or two mountains rooted fast.
sentences.n: Three similes, all in the dual. The print spells the minaret maʾdhana (مأذنة, “place of the call to prayer”); the commoner form is miʾdhana. watad, “tent-peg”, driven in with a mallet (madqūq, “pounded”). rasakha, “to be firmly rooted”.

sentences.t: فَعَرَفَ مِنْ نَفْسِهِ قِصَرَ بَاعِهِ وَنَدِمَ عَلَى الدُّنُوِّ مِنْ صِرَاعِهِ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَيْتَنِي قَاتَلْتُهُ بِسِلَاحِي
sentences.tr: fa-ʿarafa min nafsihi qiṣara bāʿihi wa-nadima ʿalā al-dunuwwi min ṣirāʿihi wa-qāla fī nafsihi laytanī qātaltuhu bi-silāḥī
sentences.l: And he knew of himself the shortness of his reach, and regretted the drawing-near to his wrestling, and said in himself: Would that I had fought him with my weapons!
sentences.i: He knew then that he was no match for him, and regretted having come to grips with him, and said to himself, “If only I had fought him with my weapons!”
sentences.n: Rhyme: bāʿihi, ṣirāʿihi. bāʿ is the span of the outstretched arms; qaṣīr al-bāʿ, “short of reach”, means weak, unequal to a task.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ قَبَضَ عَلَيْهِ وَتَمَكَّنَ مِنْهُ وَهَزَّهُ فَحَسَّ الْبَدَوِيُّ أَنَّ أَمْعَاءَهُ تَقَطَّعَتْ فِي بَطْنِهِ
