sentences.tr: thumma inna kāna mā kāna qabaḍa ʿalayhi wa-tamakkana minhu wa-hazzahu fa-ḥassa al-badawiyyu anna amʿāʾahu taqaṭṭaʿat fī baṭnihi
sentences.l: Then Kān Mā Kān seized on him and got-mastery of him and shook him, and the Bedouin felt that his guts were cut-to-pieces in his belly.
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān took hold of him, got a firm grip on him and shook him, until the Bedouin felt as though his insides were torn apart.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”: inna merely sets the new subject at the head, a common narrative shape in the Nights. ḥassa, “to feel”, stands for Classical aḥassa, a common Middle Arabic form. The print marks the doubled letters of tamakkana and ḥassa.

sentences.t: فَصَاحَ أَمْسِكْ يَدَكَ يَا غُلَامُ فَلَمْ يَلْتَفِتْ إِلَى مَا أَبْدَاةُ مِنَ الْكَلَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāḥa amsik yadaka yā ghulāmu fa-lam yaltafit ilā mā abdāhu mina al-kalāmi
sentences.l: And he cried: Hold your hand, O lad! But he did not turn to what he had shown of the speech.
sentences.i: He cried out, “Stay your hand, boy!” but Kān Mā Kān paid no heed to anything he said.
sentences.n: Rhyme: ghulām, kalām. The print writes the pronoun of abdāhu, “he put forth”, with tāʾ marbūṭa (ابداة), as it often does; read abdāhu.

sentences.t: بَلْ هَزَّةُ وَرَفَعَهُ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ وَقَصَدَ بِهِ النَّهْرَ لِيَرْمِيَهُ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: bal hazzahu wa-rafaʿahu mina al-arḍi wa-qaṣada bihi al-nahra li-yarmiyahu fīhi
sentences.l: Rather he shook him and lifted him from the ground and made with him for the river, to throw him into it.
sentences.i: Instead he shook him again, lifted him off the ground and carried him toward the river to throw him in.
sentences.n: Again the print writes the pronoun with tāʾ marbūṭa: هزّة for hazzahu, “he shook him”. qaṣada bi-, “to make for (a place) with”, that is, carrying him.

sentences.t: فَنَادَاةُ الْبَدَوِيُّ يَا أَيُّهَا الْبَطَلُ مَا الَّذِي عَزَمْتَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-nādāhu al-badawiyyu yā ayyuhā al-baṭalu mā alladhī ʿazamta ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And the Bedouin called him: O you the hero, what is it that you have resolved upon?
sentences.i: The Bedouin called out to him, “Champion, what do you mean to do?”
sentences.n: nādāhu is written with tāʾ marbūṭa (فناداة), as above.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أُرِيدُأَنْ أَرْمِيَكَ فِي هٰذَا النَّهْرِ فَهُوَ يَعْبُرُ بِكَ إِلَي الدِّجْلَةِ وَالدِّجْلَةُ تَدْخُلُ بِكَ إِلَي نَهْرِ عِيسَى وَنَهْرُ عِيسَى يُوصِلُكَ إِلَى الْفُرَاتِ وَالْفُرَاتُ يُلْقِيكَ إِلَى بِلَادِكَ فَيَرَاكَ قَوْمُكَ فَيَعْرِفُونَكَ وَيَعْرِفُونَ مُرُوَّتَكَ وَصِدْقَ مَحَبَّتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla urīdu an armiyaka fī hādhā al-nahri fa-huwa yaʿburu bika ilā al-dijlati wa-al-dijlatu tadkhulu bika ilā nahri ʿīsā wa-nahru ʿīsā yūṣiluka ilā al-furāti wa-al-furātu yulqīka ilā bilādika fa-yarāka qawmuka fa-yaʿrifūnaka wa-yaʿrifūna muruwwataka wa-ṣidqa maḥabbatika
sentences.l: And he said: I want to throw you into this river, and it will cross with you to the Tigris, and the Tigris will enter with you into the ʿĪsā Canal, and the ʿĪsā Canal will bring you to the Euphrates, and the Euphrates will cast you to your country, and your people will see you and know you, and know your manliness and the truth of your love.
sentences.i: He said, “I mean to throw you into this river. It will carry you to the Tigris, the Tigris will take you into the ʿĪsā Canal, the ʿĪsā Canal will bring you to the Euphrates, and the Euphrates will cast you up in your own country, where your people will see you and recognise you, and recognise your manly virtue and the sincerity of your love.”
sentences.n: The print runs urīdu into an (اريدان) and writes ilā twice with a dotted yāʾ (الي). The Tigris is usually Dijla without the article; here it is al-dijla. The ʿĪsā Canal joined the Euphrates to the Tigris at Baghdad, so the journey is a mocking one: the Bedouin is a Syrian, and the rivers will float him home. muruwwa, “manliness, chivalrous virtue”, is written without its hamza (مروة, Classical murūʾa).

sentences.t: فَصَاحَ صَبَّاحٌ وَنَادَي يَا فَارِسَ الْبِطَاحِ لَاتَفْعَلْ فِعْلَ الْقِبَاحِ أَطْلِقْنِي بِحَيَوٰةِ بِنْتِ عَمِّكَ زِينَةِ الْمِلَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāḥa ṣabbāḥun wa-nādā yā fārisa al-biṭāḥi lā tafʿal fiʿla al-qibāḥi aṭliqnī bi-ḥayāti binti ʿammika zīnati al-milāḥi
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ cried out and called: O horseman of the broad-valleys, do not do the doing of the vile-ones! Let me go, by the life of the daughter of your uncle, the adornment of the beauties!
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ cried out, “Knight of the open plains, do not stoop to the deeds of base men! Let me go, by the life of your cousin, the fairest of the fair!”
sentences.n: Rhyme: ṣāḥa ṣabbāḥ, biṭāḥ, qibāḥ, milāḥ; the plea runs entirely in sajʿ. biṭāḥ, plural of baṭḥāʾ, broad valleys of pebbles and sand. The print writes nādā with a dotted yāʾ (نادي), runs lā into tafʿal (لاتفعل), and spells ḥayāt in the old way with wāw and a small alif (حيوٰة). The cousin he swears by is Kān Mā Kān's, the king's daughter he has just heard of.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ وَضَعَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فِى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika waḍaʿahu kāna mā kāna fī al-arḍi
sentences.l: And at that Kān Mā Kān put him on the ground.
sentences.i: At that Kān Mā Kān set him down on the ground.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى نَفْسَهُ خَالِصًا أَتَى إِلَى سَيْفِهِ وَتُرْسِهِ وَأَخَذَهُمَا وَقَعَدَ يُشَاوِرُ نَفْسَهُ فِى الْغَدْرِ بِهِ وَالْهُجُومِ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā nafsahu khāliṣan atā ilā sayfihi wa-tursihi wa-akhadhahumā wa-qaʿada yushāwiru nafsahu fī al-ghadri bihi wa-al-hujūmi ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And when he saw himself free, he came to his sword and his shield and took them, and sat consulting himself about the treachery to him and the falling upon him.
sentences.i: When he found himself free, he went to his sword and shield and took them up, and sat there turning over in his mind whether to betray him and fall upon him.
sentences.n: khāliṣ, “free, clear (of something)”, here “let loose”. shāwara nafsahu, “to consult oneself”, to deliberate. ghadara bi-, “to act treacherously toward”: the bi- marks the victim.

sentences.t: فَعَرَفَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ مِنْ عَيْنِهِ ذٰلِكَ فَقَالَ لَهُ قَدْ عَرَفْتُ مَا فِي قَلْبِكَ حَيْثُ مَلَكْتَ سَيْفَكَ وَتُرْسَكَ وَمَالَكَ فِى الصِّرَاعِ يَدٌ طَوِيلَةٌ وَأَنْتَ عَدِيمُ الْحِيَلِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿarafa kāna mā kāna min ʿaynihi dhālika fa-qāla lahu qad ʿaraftu mā fī qalbika ḥaythu malakta sayfaka wa-tursaka wa-mā laka fī al-ṣirāʿi yadun ṭawīlatun wa-anta ʿadīmu al-ḥiyali
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān knew that from his eye, and said to him: I have known what is in your heart, since you have got-possession of your sword and your shield; and you have not in the wrestling a long hand, and you are lacking of the resources.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān read it in his eyes and said to him, “I know what is in your heart, now that you have your sword and shield in hand. You are no match for me at wrestling, and you have no other resource.
sentences.n: The print runs mā into laka (مالك), “you have not”. yad ṭawīla, “a long hand”, is power, the upper hand. ḥiyal, plural of ḥīla, “stratagem, resource”; ʿadīm, “lacking, without”.

sentences.t: وَلَوْ كُنْتَ عَلَى فَرَسٍ تَجُولُ وَبِسَيْفِكَ عَلَيَّ تَصُولُ كُنْتَ مِنْ زَمَانٍ مَقْتُولْ
sentences.tr: wa-law kunta ʿalā farasin tajūlu wa-bi-sayfika ʿalayya taṣūlu kunta min zamānin maqtūl
sentences.l: And if you were on a horse wheeling-about, and with your sword upon me assaulting, you would be from a time killed.
sentences.i: Even if you were wheeling about on horseback and charging me with your sword, you would long since be dead.
sentences.n: Rhyme: tajūlu, taṣūlu, maqtūl. Classical Arabic would say kunta maqtūlan, with the accusative; the text has the bare rhyme form, read here in pause. min zamān, “since a time”, is the colloquial “long ago, long since”. jāla, “to wheel about (in battle)”; ṣāla ʿalā, “to assault, spring upon”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أُبَلِّغُكَ مَا تَخْتَارُ حَتَّى لَايَبْقَى فِي قَلْبِكَ إِنْكَارٌ
sentences.tr: wa-anā uballighuka mā takhtāru ḥattā lā yabqā fī qalbika inkārun
sentences.l: And I will make-you-attain what you choose, so that there does not remain in your heart a denying.
sentences.i: I will give you what you wish, so that no doubt remains in your heart.
sentences.n: Rhyme: takhtāru, inkārun. ballagha, “to make (someone) reach (something)”, to grant. inkār, “denial, refusal to acknowledge”: so that he can no longer refuse to own himself beaten. The print runs lā into yabqā (لايبقى).

sentences.t: فَأَعْطِنِي التُّرْسَ وَاهْجُمْ عَلَيَّ بِسَيْفِكَ فَإِمَّا أَنْ تَقْتُلَنِي وَإِمَّا أَنْ أَقْتُلَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-aʿṭinī al-tursa wa-uhjum ʿalayya bi-sayfika fa-immā an taqtulanī wa-immā an aqtulaka
sentences.l: So give me the shield and fall upon me with your sword: either that you kill me or that I kill you.
sentences.i: So give me the shield and come at me with your sword: either you kill me or I kill you.”
sentences.n: immā … wa-immā, “either … or”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ دُونَكَ هَاهُوَ وَرَمَى لَهُ التُّرْسَ وَجَرَّدَ سَيْفَهُ وَهَجَمَ بِهِ عَلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu dūnaka hā huwa wa-ramā lahu al-tursa wa-jarrada sayfahu wa-hajama bihi ʿalā kāna mā kāna
sentences.l: And he said to him: Before you, here it is! And he threw him the shield, and bared his sword and fell with it upon Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: “There you are, take it!” said Ṣabbāḥ, and he threw him the shield, drew his sword and rushed at Kān Mā Kān with it.
sentences.n: dūnaka, “before you”, used as a command: “take it!”. The print runs hā into huwa (هاهو), “here it is”. jarrada, “to strip”, of a sword “to draw from the scabbard”.

sentences.t: فَتَنَاوَلَ التُّرْسَ بِيَمِينِهِ وَصَارَ يُلَاقِي بِهِ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-tanāwala al-tursa bi-yamīnihi wa-ṣāra yulāqī bihi ʿan nafsihi
sentences.l: And he took the shield in his right-hand, and began meeting (the blows) with it from himself.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān caught the shield in his right hand and began to fend off the blows with it.
sentences.n: lāqā, “to meet, encounter”; with ʿan nafsihi, “away from himself”, it is used here for warding off, a sense the dictionaries give to other verbs (ittaqā, “to shield oneself”). ṣāra, “he became”, before a verb means “he began to”, a turn the text uses constantly.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ صَبَّاحٌ يَضْرِبُهُ وَيَقُولُ لَهُ مَابَقِيَ إِلَّا هٰذِةِ الضَّرْبَةُ الْفَاضِلَةُ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra ṣabbāḥun yaḍribuhu wa-yaqūlu lahu mā baqiya illā hādhihi al-ḍarbatu al-fāḍilatu
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ began striking him and saying to him: There has not remained but this blow, the surpassing-one!
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ kept striking at him and saying, “Only this one left, the master-stroke!”
sentences.n: The print runs mā into baqiya (مابقي) and writes hādhihi with tāʾ marbūṭa (هذة), as it habitually does. al-fāḍila, “the excellent, surpassing” (also “the left-over”), is kept as printed; the sense wanted may well be al-fāṣila, “the decisive, the one that settles it” (الفاصلة, one dot different), but the print's word can stand.

sentences.t: فَتَخْرُجُ غَيْرَ قَاتِلَةٍ وَيَأْخُذُهَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ فِى التُّرْسِ وَتَرُوحُ ضَائِعَةً وَلَا يَضْرِبُهُ لِأَنَّ مَا مَعَهُ شَيْءٌ يَضْرِبُ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-takhruju ghayra qātilatin wa-yaʾkhudhuhā kāna mā kāna fī al-tursi wa-tarūḥu ḍāʾiʿatan wa-lā yaḍribuhu li-anna mā maʿahu shayʾun yaḍribu bihi
sentences.l: And it would come-out not killing, and Kān Mā Kān would take it on the shield and it would go wasted; and he did not strike him, because not with him a thing he might strike with.
sentences.i: But each one fell short of killing: Kān Mā Kān took it on the shield and it went for nothing. He did not strike back, for he had nothing to strike with.
sentences.n: Rhyme: qātila, ḍāʾiʿa. rāḥa, “to go”, colloquial for “to go off, end up”. li-anna mā maʿahu, “because not with him”: Classical Arabic would say li-annahu laysa maʿahu; the text puts the negative mā straight after anna, a Middle Arabic habit. The print sets a sukūn on the ḍ of yaḍribuhu.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ صَبَّاحٌ يَضْرِبُهُ بِالسَّيْفِ حَتَّى كَلَّتْ يَدُةُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal ṣabbāḥun yaḍribuhu bi-al-sayfi ḥattā kallat yaduhu
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ did not cease striking him with the sword until his hand grew-tired.
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ went on hacking at him with the sword until his arm was weary.
sentences.n: lam yazal, “did not cease”, with a verb: “kept on doing”. kalla, “to grow tired, blunt”. The print writes the pronoun of yaduhu, “his hand”, with tāʾ marbūṭa (يدة).

sentences.t: وَعَرَفَ خَصْمُهُ مِنْهُ ذٰلِكَ فَهَجَمَ عَلَيْهِ وَاحْتَضَنَهُ وَهَزَّةُ وَأَلْقَاهُ فِى الْأَرْضِ وَأَدَارَ كِتَافَهُ وَكَتَّفَهُ بِحَمَائِلِ سَيْفِهِ وَجَرَّةُ مِنْ رِجْلَيْهِ وَقَصَدَ بِهِ النَّهْرَ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿarafa khaṣmuhu minhu dhālika fa-hajama ʿalayhi wa-iḥtaḍanahu wa-hazzahu wa-alqāhu fī al-arḍi wa-adāra kitāfahu wa-kattafahu bi-ḥamāʾili sayfihi wa-jarrahu min rijlayhi wa-qaṣada bihi al-nahra
sentences.l: And his adversary knew that from him, and fell upon him and hugged him and shook him and threw him on the ground, and turned his shoulder-bonds and bound-his-arms with the baldric-straps of his sword, and dragged him by his feet and made with him for the river.
sentences.i: His opponent saw it, and fell on him, seized him in his arms, shook him and threw him to the ground; then he pulled his arms behind his back, tied them with the straps of his own sword-belt, dragged him off by the feet and made for the river.
sentences.n: adāra kitāfahu, “he turned his bonds”, the same phrase Ṣabbāḥ used when he ordered Kān Mā Kān to put his hands behind his back for tying; now the order is turned on him. kitāf is the rope that binds the arms at the shoulders (katif); kattafa, “to bind the arms behind the back”. ḥamāʾil, “the straps from which a sword is slung”. The print again writes the pronoun with tāʾ marbūṭa in هزّة, hazzahu, and جرّة, jarrahu.

sentences.t: فَنَادَاةُ صَبَّاحٌ أَيُّ شَيْءٍ تُرِيدُ تَصْنَعُ بِي أَيُّهَا الشَّابُّ وَفَارِسَ الزَّمَانِ وَبَطَلَ الْمَيْدَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-nādāhu ṣabbāḥun ayyu shayʾin turīdu taṣnaʿu bī ayyuhā al-shābbu wa-fārisa al-zamāni wa-baṭala al-maydāni
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ called him: What thing do you want (to) do with me, O you the young-man, and horseman of the age and hero of the field?
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ called out to him, “What do you mean to do with me, young man, knight of the age, champion of the field?”
sentences.n: Rhyme: zamān, maydān. turīdu taṣnaʿu, “you want you do”: the text sets the second verb straight after the first with no an, as the spoken language does. ayyu shayʾin, “what thing”, is the full form of colloquial aysh, “what”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكَ إِنَّ قَصْدِي أَنْ أُرْسِلَكَ إِلَى أَهْلِكَ وَقَوْمِكَ فِى النَّهْرِ حَتَّى لَا يَشْتَغِلَ خَاطِرُكَ وَلَا خَاطِرُهُمْ عَلَيْكَ وَتَتَعَوَّقَ عَنْ عُرْسِ ابْنَةِ عَمِّكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu a-lam aqul laka inna qaṣdī an ursilaka ilā ahlika wa-qawmika fī al-nahri ḥattā lā yashtaghila khāṭiruka wa-lā khāṭiruhum ʿalayka wa-tataʿawwaqa ʿan ʿursi ibnati ʿammika
sentences.l: And he said to him: Did I not tell you that my purpose is that I send you to your family and your people in the river, so that your mind will not be occupied, nor their mind about you, and (that) you be held-back from the wedding of the daughter of your uncle?
sentences.i: He said to him, “Did I not tell you that I mean to send you home to your family and your people by way of the river, so that neither you nor they need worry about each other, and you will not be kept from your cousin's wedding?”
sentences.n: ishtaghala khāṭiruhu ʿalā, “his mind was taken up with (someone)”, to be anxious about. taʿawwaqa ʿan, “to be held back from”, a post-classical form from ʿāqa, “to hinder”. The negative lā is understood again before tataʿawwaqa: he will not be late for the wedding. The mockery is open: Najma is waiting, and the river will get him there.

sentences.t: فَضَجَّرَ صَبَّاحٌ وَبَكَى وَصَاحَ وَقَالَ لَاتَفْعَلْ يَا فَارِسَ الزَّمَانِ وَأَطْلِقْنِي وَاجْعَلْنِي لَكَ مِنْ بَعْضِ الْغِلْمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍajjara ṣabbāḥun wa-bakā wa-ṣāḥa wa-qāla lā tafʿal yā fārisa al-zamāni wa-aṭliqnī wa-ijʿalnī laka min baʿḍi al-ghilmāni
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ grew-distressed and wept and cried-out and said: Do not do (it), O horseman of the age! And let me go, and make me for you (one) of some of the pages.
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ, in his distress, wept and cried aloud and said, “Do not do it, knight of the age! Let me go, and make me one of your servants.”
sentences.n: Rhyme: zamān, ghilmān. The print sets a doubled jīm in فضجّر. The verb ḍajjara is properly transitive, “to vex”, and the sense here is plainly “he grew vexed, distressed”, Classical ḍajira; the doubling may be the print's slip, or the text may use the form intransitively. Another possibility is ḍajja, “he cried out”, with a stray rāʾ. It is kept as printed. ghilmān, plural of ghulām, “lad, page, slave”: the Bedouin now offers to be what he had meant to make of Kān Mā Kān.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى وَاشْتَكَى وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: thumma bakā wa-ishtakā wa-anshada yaqūlu shiʿrun
sentences.l: Then he wept and complained, and recited, saying: verse.
sentences.i: Then he wept and lamented, and recited these lines:
sentences.n: Rhyme: bakā, ishtakā. shiʿr, “verse”, stands in the print as a heading for the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
تَغَرَّبْتُ عَنْ اَهْلِي فَيَاطُولَ غُرْبَتِي * وَيَالَيْتَ شِعْرِي هَلْ اَمُوتُ غَرِيبًا
اَمُوتُ وَاَهْلِي لَيْسَ يَعْرِفُ مَقْتَلِي * وَاَوْدَى غَرِيبًا لَا اَزُورُ حَبِيبًا
sentences.tr:
tagharrabtu ʿan ahlī fa-yā ṭūla ghurbatī * wa-yā layta shiʿrī hal amūtu gharībā
amūtu wa-ahlī laysa yaʿrifu maqtalī * wa-awdā gharīban lā azūru ḥabībā
sentences.l:
I have gone-abroad from my people, and O the length of my exile! * And O would that my knowing (were): shall I die a stranger?
I shall die, and my people do not know the place-of-my-killing, * and I shall perish a stranger, not visiting a beloved.
sentences.i:
I have wandered far from my people: how long my exile! * Would that I knew: shall I die a stranger?
I shall die, and my kin will not know where I was slain, * and perish far from home, with no beloved to visit.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre ṭawīl, rhyming in -bā, copied as the print points them. The print runs yā into ṭūla (فياطول) and into layta (وياليت). yā ṭūla ghurbatī, “O the length of my exile!”, is an exclamation of grief. layta shiʿrī, “would that my knowing”, is the standing idiom for “I wish I knew”: shiʿr here is “knowledge, awareness”, not “poetry”. maqtal, “the place (or manner) of being killed”. awdā, “to perish”. The word gharīb, “stranger”, closes the first line and comes back inside the second, a deliberate echo.

sentences.t: فَرَحِمَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ تُعَاهِدُنِي بِالْعُهُودِ وَالْمَوَاثِيقِ عَلَى أَنَّكَ تَكُونُ لِي نِعْمَ الرَّفِيقُ وَتَصْحَبُنِي فِي كُلِّ طَرِيقٍ فَقَالَ نَعَمْ وَعَاهَدَةُ عَلَى ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-raḥimahu kāna mā kāna wa-qāla lahu tuʿāhidunī bi-al-ʿuhūdi wa-al-mawāthīqi ʿalā annaka takūnu lī niʿma al-rafīqu wa-taṣḥabunī fī kulli ṭarīqin fa-qāla naʿam wa-ʿāhadahu ʿalā dhālika
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān took-pity on him and said to him: You pledge me with the pledges and the covenants that you will be to me the best of companions and accompany me on every road. And he said: Yes; and he pledged him to that.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān took pity on him and said, “Give me your solemn word and covenant that you will be the best of companions to me and keep me company on every road.” “Yes,” said he, and swore it to him.
sentences.n: tuʿāhidunī, “you pledge me”, is an indicative used as a request: “you will swear to me”. ʿuhūd and mawāthīq, “pledges and covenants”, a stock pair. niʿma al-rafīq, “how excellent a companion!”: niʿma is the verb of praise, so its noun stays nominative inside the clause. Rhyme: rafīq, ṭarīq. وعاهدة is ʿāhadahu, ة for -hu again.

sentences.t: فَأَطْلَقَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَقَامَ صَبَّاحٌ وَأَرَادَأَنْ يُقَبِّلَ يَدَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَمَنَعَهُ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭlaqahu kāna mā kāna fa-qāma ṣabbāḥun wa-arāda an yuqabbila yada kāna mā kāna fa-manaʿahu min dhālika
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān released him; and Ṣabbāḥ rose and wanted to kiss the hand of Kān Mā Kān, and he prevented him from that.
sentences.i: So Kān Mā Kān let him go. Ṣabbāḥ got up and would have kissed his hand, but Kān Mā Kān would not allow it.
sentences.n: The print runs arāda into an (وارادان), read wa-arāda an, “and he wanted to”. Kissing the hand is the gesture of a client to his patron; Kān Mā Kān refuses it as from an equal.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْبَدَوِى وَفَتَحَ جِرَابَهُ وَأَخْرَجَ مِنْهُ ثَلٰثَ قُرْصَاتِ شَعِيرٍ وَوَضَعَهَا قُدَّامَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَجَلَسَ هُوَ وَإِيَّاةُ عَلَى حَافَةِ النَّهْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-badawī wa-fataḥa jirābahu wa-akhraja minhu thalātha qurṣāti shaʿīrin wa-waḍaʿahā quddāma kāna mā kāna wa-jalasa huwa wa-iyyāhu ʿalā ḥāfati al-nahri
sentences.l: And the Bedouin rose and opened his bag and brought out from it three round-loaves of barley, and put them before Kān Mā Kān; and he sat, he and him, on the edge of the river.
sentences.i: Then the Bedouin got up, opened his provision bag and took out three barley cakes, which he set before Kān Mā Kān, and the two of them sat down together on the riverbank.
sentences.n: The print writes badawī with a dotless yāʾ (البدوى). jirāb, a leather bag for provisions. thalāth is spelled defectively, with the small alif over the lām, as the print sets it. qurṣa (plural qurṣāt) is a round flat loaf; qurṣāt shaʿīr, “loaves of barley”, the poor man's bread. huwa wa-iyyāhu, “he and him”, is a colloquial way of saying “the two of them together”, and the print writes iyyāhu with tāʾ marbūṭa for the final hāʾ (واياة).

sentences.t: وَأَكَلَ الِاثْنَانِ مَعَ بَعْضِهِمَا وَلَمَّا فَرَغَا مِنَ الْأَكْلِ تَوَضَّأَا وَصَلَّيَا وَجَلَسَا يَتَحَدَّثَانِ عَلَى مَالَقِيَاةُ مِنْ أَهْلِهِمَا وَمِنْ صُرُوفِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-akala al-ithnāni maʿa baʿḍihimā wa-lammā faraghā mina al-akli tawaḍḍaʾā wa-ṣallayā wa-jalasā yataḥaddathāni ʿalā mā laqiyāhu min ahlihimā wa-min ṣurūfi al-zamāni
sentences.l: And the two ate with each-other, and when they had finished from the eating, they performed-the-ablution and prayed, and sat talking about what they had met from their families and from the turns of the time.
sentences.i: The two ate together, and when they had finished their meal they washed for prayer and prayed, and then sat talking of what they had suffered from their families and from the shifts of fortune.
sentences.n: maʿa baʿḍihimā, “with each other”, is the colloquial idiom for “together”. tawaḍḍaʾā, “they performed the ablution (wuḍūʾ)”, the washing before prayer. taḥaddatha ʿalā, “to talk about”, where Classical prefers ʿan or fī. The print runs mā into laqiyāhu (مالقياة), “what the two of them met with”, and again writes the pronoun -hu with tāʾ marbūṭa. ṣurūf al-zamān, “the turns of time”, the reversals of fortune.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِلَى أَيْنَ تَعْزِمُ فَقَالَ صَبَّاحٌ عَزْمِي إِلَى بَغْدَادَ بَلَدِكَ أُقِيمُ بِهَا حَتَّى يَرْزُقَ اللّٰهُ لِي بِالصَّدَاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu kāna mā kāna ilā ayna taʿzimu fa-qāla ṣabbāḥun ʿazmī ilā baghdāda baladika uqīmu bihā ḥattā yarzuqa allāhu lī bi-al-ṣadāqi
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to him: To where do you resolve? And Ṣabbāḥ said: My resolve (is) to Baghdad, your city; I shall stay in it until God provides for me with the bride-price.
sentences.i: “Where are you bound?” Kān Mā Kān asked him. Ṣabbāḥ said, “I am making for Baghdad, your city, to stay there until God provides me with the bride-price.”
sentences.n: ʿazama ilā, “to set out resolutely for”. ṣadāq is the marriage gift a man pays to his bride; Ṣabbāḥ needs it to marry his cousin Najma. razaqa, “to provide”, normally takes two direct objects (razaqahu al-ṣadāqa); here the text says razaqa lī bi-, “provide for me with”, a looser, colloquial construction.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ دُونَكَ وَالطَّرِيقَ وَهَا أَنَا هُنَا فَوَدَّعَهُ الْبَدَوِيُّ وَطَلَبَ طَرِيقَ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu dūnaka wa-al-ṭarīqa wa-hā anā hunā fa-waddaʿahu al-badawiyyu wa-ṭalaba ṭarīqa baghdāda
sentences.l: And he said to him: Before you, and the road! And here I am, here. And the Bedouin bade him farewell and sought the road of Baghdad.
sentences.i: “The road is yours,” said Kān Mā Kān, “and here I stay.” So the Bedouin took his leave of him and set off on the road to Baghdad.
sentences.n: dūnaka, “before you”, used as an imperative: “take it, it is yours”; wa-al-ṭarīqa, “and the road”, is in the accusative as the thing offered. wa-hā anā hunā, “and here I am, here”: Kān Mā Kān stays behind. ṭalaba al-ṭarīq, “to seek the road”, to set out along it.

sentences.t: وَقَامَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ يَا نَفْسِي أَيُّ وَجْهٍ لِلرُّجُوعِ مَعَ الْفَقْرِ وَالْفَاقَةِ فَوَاللّٰهِ لَا أَرْجِعُ خَائِبًا وَلَا بُدَّلِي مِنَ الْفَرَجِ إِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: wa-qāma kāna mā kāna wa-qāla fī nafsihi yā nafsī ayyu wajhin li-al-rujūʿi maʿa al-faqri wa-al-fāqati fa-wa-allāhi lā arjiʿu khāʾiban wa-lā budda lī mina al-faraji in shāʾa allāhu taʿālā
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān rose and said in himself: O my soul, what face (is there) for the returning with the poverty and the want? For by God, I shall not return disappointed, and there is no escape for me from the relief, if God wills, He the Exalted.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān got up and said to himself, “My soul, with what face could I go back, poor and in want? By God, I will not return empty-handed: relief must surely come to me, if God, the Exalted, wills.”
sentences.n: ayyu wajhin li-al-rujūʿ, “what face is there for returning?”: how could I show my face if I went back. faqr and fāqa, “poverty and want”, another near-synonymous pair. The print runs budda into lī (بدلي): lā budda lī min, “there is no escape for me from”, that is, it must come to me. faraj, “relief, release from trouble”, the word for a happy turn of fortune.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَ إِلَى النَّهْرِ وَتَوَضَّأَ وَصَلَّى
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddama ilā al-nahri wa-tawaḍḍaʾa wa-ṣallā
sentences.l: Then he went-forward to the river and performed-the-ablution and prayed.
sentences.i: Then he went down to the river, washed for prayer, and prayed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَجَدَ وَوَضَعَ جَبْهَتَهُ عَلَى التُّرَابِ نَادَى رَبَّهُ وَقَالَ اللّٰهُمَّ مُنْزِلَ الْقَطْرِ وَرَازِقَ الدُّودِ فِى الْحَجَرِ أَسْأَلُكَ أَنْ تَرْزُقَنِي بِقُدْرَتِكَ وَلَطِيفِ رَحْمَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā sajada wa-waḍaʿa jabhatahu ʿalā al-turābi nādā rabbahu wa-qāla allāhumma munzila al-qaṭri wa-rāziqa al-dūdi fī al-ḥajari asʾaluka an tarzuqanī bi-qudratika wa-laṭīfi raḥmatika
sentences.l: And when he prostrated and put his forehead on the dust, he called his Lord and said: O God, sender-down of the rain-drops and provider of the worm in the stone, I ask you to provide for me by your power and the gentleness of your mercy.
sentences.i: When he bowed down and laid his forehead in the dust, he called upon his Lord and said, “O God, who send down the rain and feed the worm inside the rock, I ask you to provide for me by your power and your gentle mercy.”
sentences.n: allāhumma, “O God”, the vocative form used in prayer; the titles that follow are in the accusative as further vocatives. qaṭr, “drops”, the rain. God who feeds the worm in the stone is a proverbial picture of providence reaching where nothing could. laṭīf raḥmatika, “the gentle of your mercy”: the adjective is set before the noun it qualifies, a frequent turn in prayers.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَلَّمَ مِنْ صَلَوٰتِهِ وَضَاقَ بِهِ كُلُّ مَسْلَكٍ
sentences.tr: thumma sallama min ṣalātihi wa-ḍāqa bihi kullu maslakin
sentences.l: Then he gave-the-salutation from his prayer, and every path became-narrow for him.
sentences.i: Then he ended his prayer with the salutation; and every way seemed closed to him.
sentences.n: sallama, “to say al-salāmu ʿalaykum”, the greeting that closes the ritual prayer. The print spells ṣalāt in the old way, with wāw and the small alif (صلوٰته). ḍāqa bihi, “became narrow on him”: he could see no way out.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ جَالِسٌ يَلْتَفِتُ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا وَإِذَا بِفَارِسٍ أَقْبَلَ عَلَى جَوَادٍ وَقَدِ اقْتَعَدَ ظَهْرَهُ وَأَرْخَي عِنَانَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa jālisun yaltafitu yamīnan wa-shimālan wa-idhā bi-fārisin aqbala ʿalā jawādin wa-qadi iqtaʿada ẓahrahu wa-arkhā ʿinānahu
sentences.l: And while he was sitting, turning right and left, and behold, a horseman came-up on a steed; and he had sat-firm on its back and let-loose its rein.
sentences.i: As he sat there looking about him to right and left, a horseman came riding up on a fine horse, seated on its back with the rein let fall slack.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: bi- marks what suddenly appears. jawād, a horse of quality, a courser. iqtaʿada, “to take as a mount, sit firmly on”. The print writes arkhā with a dotted yāʾ (ارخي). arkhā al-ʿinān, “to slacken the rein”, to let the horse run as it will; here, as the next sentences show, because the rider can no longer hold it.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَوَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ جَالِسًا
sentences.tr: fa-istawā kāna mā kāna jālisan
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān straightened-up sitting.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān sat up straight.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ وَصَلَ إِلَيْهِ الْفَارِسُ وَهُوَ فِي آخِرِ نَفَسٍ وَقَدْ أَيْقَنَ بِالْفَنَاءِ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ بِهِ جُرْحٌ بَالِغٌ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda sāʿatin waṣala ilayhi al-fārisu wa-huwa fī ākhiri nafasin wa-qad ayqana bi-al-fanāʾi li-annahu kāna bihi jurḥun bālighun
sentences.l: And after an hour the horseman reached him, and he (was) at the last breath and had become-certain of the perishing, because there was on him a wound severe.
sentences.i: A little while later the horseman reached him. He was at his last gasp and sure that he was dying, for he had a grievous wound.
sentences.n: sāʿa, “an hour”, often only “a while”. nafas, “breath”; fī ākhiri nafas, “at his last breath”. ayqana bi-, “to be certain of”. bāligh, “reaching (far)”, of a wound: deep, grave.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَيْهِ جَرِي دَمْعُهُ عَلِي خَدِّهِ مِثْلَ أَفْوَاهِ الْقِرَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣala ilayhi jarā damʿuhu ʿalā khaddihi mithla afwāhi al-qirabi
sentences.l: And when he reached him, his tears ran on his cheek like the mouths of the waterskins.
sentences.i: When he came up to him, his tears ran down his cheek like water pouring from the mouths of waterskins.
sentences.n: The print writes jarā and ʿalā with a dotted yāʾ (جري, علي). qirab, plural of qirba, “waterskin”: the tears gush as from an unstopped skin, a common hyperbole.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لِكَانَ مَا كَانَ يَا وَجْهَ الْعَرَبِ اتَّخِذْنِي مَا عِشْتُ لَكَ صَدِيقًا فَإِنَّكَ لَا تَجِدُ مِثْلِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla li-kāna mā kāna yā wajha al-ʿarabi ittakhidhnī mā ʿishtu laka ṣadīqan fa-innaka lā tajidu mithlī
sentences.l: And he said to Kān Mā Kān: O face of the Arabs, take me, as long as I live, for you a friend, for you will not find the like of me.
sentences.i: And he said to Kān Mā Kān, “Noblest of the Arabs, take me for your friend as long as I live, for you will not find another like me.
sentences.n: The print splits the name after li-, “to” (لكان | ما كان). wajh al-ʿArab, “face of the Arabs”, the best and most honoured of them, a flattering form of address; the rhyme qirab, ʿarab joins this to the sentence before. ittakhadha … ṣadīqan, “to take as a friend”; the print marks the doubled tāʾ. mā ʿishtu, “as long as I live”.

sentences.t: وَاسْقِنِي قَلِيلًا مِنَ الْمَاءِ وَإِنْ كَانَ شُرْبُ الْمَاءِ لَا يَصْلُحُ لِلْمَجْرُوحِ سِيَّمَا وَقْتَ خُرُوجِ الدَّمِ وَالرُّوحِ
sentences.tr: wa-isqinī qalīlan mina al-māʾi wa-in kāna shurbu al-māʾi lā yaṣluḥu li-al-majrūḥi siyyamā waqta khurūji al-dami wa-al-rūḥi
sentences.l: And give-me-to-drink a little of the water, even if the drinking of the water is not good for the wounded, especially the time of the going-out of the blood and the spirit.
sentences.i: Give me a little water to drink, though water is bad for a wounded man, above all when his blood and his life are ebbing away.
sentences.n: wa-in kāna, “even if”. The print marks the ḍamma of shurbu itself. siyyamā, “especially”, stands here without its usual lā (Classical lā siyyamā), a common shortening. Rhyme: majrūḥ, rūḥ; khurūj al-rūḥ, “the going out of the spirit”, is death.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ عِشْتُ دَفَعْتُ لَكَ مَا يَجْبُرُ كَسْرَكَ وَفَقْرَكَ وَإِنْ مُتُّ فَأَنْتَ الْمَسْعُودُ بِحُسْنِ نِيَّتِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-in ʿishtu dafaʿtu laka mā yajburu kasraka wa-faqraka wa-in muttu fa-anta al-masʿūdu bi-ḥusni niyyatika
sentences.l: And if I live, I shall pay to you what sets your break and your poverty; and if I die, then you are the fortunate-one by the goodness of your intention.
sentences.i: If I live, I will give you enough to mend your broken fortunes and your poverty; and if I die, you will still be blessed for your good intent.”
sentences.n: jabara al-kasr, “to set a broken bone”, hence to restore someone's fortunes; kasr and faqr rhyme in sound. dafaʿa li-, “to pay to, hand over to”, where Classical would usually say dafaʿa ilā. al-masʿūd, “the fortunate one”, here the one rewarded by God for a good deed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ تَحْتَ ذٰلِكَ الْفَارِسِ جَوَادٌ مِنْ جِيَادِ الْحِصَانِ يَكِلُّ عَنْ وَصْفِّهِ اللِّسَانُ وَلَهُ قَوَائِمُ مِثْلُ أَعْمِدَةِ الرُّخَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna taḥta dhālika al-fārisi jawādun min jiyādi al-ḥiṣāni yakillu ʿan waṣfihi al-lisānu wa-lahu qawāʾimu mithlu aʿmidati al-rukhāmi
sentences.l: And under that horseman was a steed of the steeds of the horse, the tongue grows-weary from its describing, and it had legs like columns of the marble.
sentences.i: Under the horseman was a horse of the noblest breed, one beyond all power of words to describe, with legs like marble columns.
sentences.n: jiyād, plural of jawād, “steeds”; jiyād al-ḥiṣān, “the best of horses”. ḥiṣān is properly a stallion. Rhyme: ḥiṣān, lisān. kalla ʿan, “to be too weary for, fall short of”. The print sets a shadda over the fāʾ of waṣfihi, “its description” (وصفّه); the word has no doubled letter, and the mark looks stray. qawāʾim, “legs”, literally “the things it stands on”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ إِلَيْهِ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَإِلَى ذٰلِكَ الْحِصَانِ أَخَذَهُ الْهَيَمَانُ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِنَّ مِثْلَ هٰذَا الْحِصَانِ لَا يُوجَدُ فِي هٰذَا الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara ilayhi kāna mā kāna wa-ilā dhālika al-ḥiṣāni akhadhahu al-hayamānu wa-qāla fī nafsihi inna mithla hādhā al-ḥiṣāni lā yūjadu fī hādhā al-zamāni
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān looked at him and at that horse, the infatuation took him, and he said in himself: Truly the like of this horse is not found in this time.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān looked at the rider and at that horse, he was seized with longing, and he said to himself, “There is not another horse like this one in all the world today.”
sentences.n: hayamān, “passionate distraction”, the word for the bewildered longing of lovers; here it is the horse that Kān Mā Kān falls for. Rhyme: ḥiṣān, hayamān, zamān.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ أَنْزَلَ الْفَارِسَ وَرَفَقَ بِهِ وَجَرَّعَهُ يَسِيرًا مِنَ الْمَاءِ وَصَبَرَ عَلَيْهِ حَتَّي أَخَذَ الرَّاحَةَ وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَيْهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ مَنِ الَّذِي فَعَلَ بِكَ هٰذِهِ الْفِعَالَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu anzala al-fārisa wa-rafaqa bihi wa-jarraʿahu yasīran mina al-māʾi wa-ṣabara ʿalayhi ḥattā akhadha al-rāḥata wa-aqbala ʿalayhi wa-qāla lahu mani alladhī faʿala bika hādhihi al-fiʿāla
sentences.l: Then he brought-down the horseman and was-gentle with him, and made-him-sip a little of the water, and was-patient with him until he took the rest; and he turned to him and said to him: Who (is) the one who did to you these deeds?
sentences.i: Then he helped the horseman down, treated him gently and gave him a few sips of water, and waited patiently by him until he had rested. Then he turned to him and asked, “Who has done this to you?”
sentences.n: rafaqa bi-, “to be gentle with”. jarraʿa, “to make someone gulp, give him sips”; the print marks the doubled rāʾ. The print writes ḥattā with a dotted yāʾ (حتي). aqbala ʿalā, “to turn one's attention to”. fiʿāl, “doings, deeds”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْفَارِسُ أَنَا أُخْبِرُكَ بِحَقِيقَةِ الْحَالِ أَنَا رَجُلٌ سَلَّالٌ غَيَّارٌ طُولَ دَهْرِي أَسُلُّ الْخَيْلَ وَأَخْتَلِسُهَا فِى اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ وَأَنَا يُقَالُ لِي غَسَّانُ آفَةُ كُلِّ حِجْرَةٍ وَحِصَانٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-fārisu anā ukhbiruka bi-ḥaqīqati al-ḥāli anā rajulun sallālun ghayyārun ṭūla dahrī asullu al-khayla wa-akhtalisuhā fī al-layli wa-al-nahāri wa-anā yuqālu lī ghassānu āfatu kulli ḥijratin wa-ḥiṣānin
sentences.l: And the horseman said: I inform you of the truth of the situation. I am a man, a filcher, a raider, the length of my lifetime; I filch the horses and snatch them in the night and the day; and I, it is said to me: Ghassān, the bane of every mare and stallion.
sentences.i: The horseman said, “I will tell you how things truly stand. I am a horse-thief and a raider, and have been all my life: I steal horses and spirit them away by night and by day, and men call me Ghassān, the bane of every mare and stallion.
sentences.n: Rhyme: ḥāl, sallāl. sallāl, from salla, “to draw out stealthily”, is a thief who slips things away; the print marks the doubled lām of asullu. ghayyār is less clear: most likely “raider”, from ghāra, “a raid”, though it could be linked with ghāra, “to be jealous”, which suits a thief poorly. ikhtalasa, “to snatch, make off with”. yuqālu lī, “it is said to me”, that is, I am called. āfa, “bane, blight”. ḥijra for “mare” is a post-classical form of ḥijr; ḥijra and ḥiṣān, mare and stallion, make a pair.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ سَمِعْتُ بِهٰذَا الْحِصَانِ فِي بِلَادِ الرُّومِ عِنْدَ الْمَلِكِ أَفْرِيدُونَ وَقَدْ سَمَّاهُ بِالْقَاتُولِ وَلَقَّبَهُ بِالْمَجْنُونِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad samiʿtu bi-hādhā al-ḥiṣāni fī bilādi al-rūmi ʿinda al-maliki afrīdūna wa-qad sammāhu bi-al-qātūli wa-laqqabahu bi-al-majnūni
sentences.l: And I had heard of this horse in the land of the Rūm, with King Afrīdūn, and he had named it al-Qātūl and surnamed it al-Majnūn.
sentences.i: I had heard of this horse in the land of the Byzantines, in the keeping of King Afrīdūn, who had named it al-Qātūl, the Killer, and given it the byname al-Majnūn, the Madman.
sentences.n: samiʿa bi-, “to hear of”. al-Rūm, the Byzantines. qātūl, an intensive form, “the great killer”. sammā bi- and laqqaba bi-, “to name” and “to give a byname”: bi- marks the name given; the print marks the doubled qāf. Rhyme: Afrīdūn, al-Majnūn.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ كُنْتُ سَافَرْتُ إِلَى الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ مِنْ أَجْلِهِ وَصِرْتُ أُرَاقِبُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qad kuntu sāfartu ilā al-qusṭanṭīniyyati min ajlihi wa-ṣirtu urāqibuhu
sentences.l: And I had travelled to al-Qusṭanṭīniyya for its sake, and I began watching it.
sentences.i: So I had made the journey to Constantinople for its sake, and began to watch for my chance at it.
sentences.n: kuntu sāfartu, “I had travelled”: kāna with a perfect gives a pluperfect. ṣāra with an imperfect, “to begin to, take to”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا أَنَا كَذٰلِكَ إِذْ خَرَجَتْ عَجُوزٌ مُعَظَّمَةٌ عِنْدَ الرُّومِ وَأَمْرُهَا عِنْدَهُمْ نَافِذٌ تُسَمَّى شَوَاهِي ذَاتَ الدَّوَاهِي وَهِيَ فِى الْخِدَاعِ مُتَنَاهِي
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā anā ka-dhālika idh kharajat ʿajūzun muʿaẓẓamatun ʿinda al-rūmi wa-amruhā ʿindahum nāfidhun tusammā shawāhī dhāta al-dawāhī wa-hiya fī al-khidāʿi mutanāhī
sentences.l: And while I was thus, behold, there came out an old-woman, revered among the Rūm, and her command among them (was) effective, (who) is named Shawāhī Dhāt al-Dawāhī, and she (was) in the deceiving reaching-the-limit.
sentences.i: While I was so engaged, out came an old woman, held in great honour among the Byzantines, whose word was law to them, named Shawāhī Dhāt al-Dawāhī, “Mistress of Calamities”, and she was the very last word in cunning.
sentences.n: nāfidh, “piercing, carried out”, of a command that is obeyed. dawāhī, plural of dāhiya, “calamity”, and also “a cunning schemer”; her byname plays on both. Rhyme: Shawāhī, al-dawāhī, mutanāhī. mutanāhī, “reaching the utmost”, is masculine where a woman would need mutanāhiya; the rhyme has won over agreement.

sentences.t: وَمَعَهَا هٰذَا الْجَوَادُ وَصُحْبَتَهَا عَشَرَةُ عَبِيدٍ لَاغَيْرُ وَهُمْ بِرَسْمِ خِدْمَتِهَا وَالْحِصَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-maʿahā hādhā al-jawādu wa-ṣuḥbatahā ʿasharatu ʿabīdin lā ghayru wa-hum bi-rasmi khidmatihā wa-al-ḥiṣāni
sentences.l: And with her (was) this steed, and in-her-company ten slaves, not other, and they (were) by assignment of the service of her and the horse.
sentences.i: She had this horse with her and an escort of ten slaves, no more, whose charge was to serve her and the horse.
sentences.n: ṣuḥbatahā, “in her company”, used as a preposition, as before. The print runs lā into ghayr (لاغير): lā ghayru, “and no more”. bi-rasm, “by assignment to, appointed for”, a chancery phrase.

sentences.t: وَقَصَدَتْ هِيَ بَغْدَادَ وَخُرَاسَانَ وَتُرِيدُ الدُّخُولَ عَلَى الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ لِتَطْلُبَ مِنْهُ الصُّلْحَ وَالْأَمَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-qaṣadat hiya baghdāda wa-khurāsāna wa-turīdu al-dukhūla ʿalā al-maliki sāsāna li-taṭluba minhu al-ṣulḥa wa-al-amāna
sentences.l: And she made-for Baghdad and Khurāsān, and wants the entering upon al-Malik Sāsān, to seek from him the peace and the safety.
sentences.i: She was bound for Baghdad and Khurāsān, meaning to gain audience with al-Malik Sāsān and ask him for peace and a guarantee of safety.
sentences.n: Rhyme: Khurāsān, Sāsān, amān. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to” a ruler, to be received by him. The tenses move from past to present (turīdu), as told speech often does. ṣulḥ, “peace, a truce”; amān, “safe-conduct, guarantee of protection”.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجْتُ فِي أَثَرِهِمْ طَمَعًا فِى الْحِصَانِ وَمَازِلْتُ تَابِعَهُمْ وَلَا أَقْدِرُ أَصِلُ إِلَيْهِ لِأَنَّ الْعَبِيدَ شِدَادُ الْحِرْصِ عَلَيْهِ إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلُوا إِلَى تِلْكَ الْبِلَادِ وَخِفْتُ أَنْ يَدْخُلُوا مَدِينَةَ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajtu fī atharihim ṭamaʿan fī al-ḥiṣāni wa-mā ziltu tābiʿahum wa-lā aqdiru aṣilu ilayhi li-anna al-ʿabīda shidādu al-ḥirṣi ʿalayhi ilā an waṣalū ilā tilka al-bilādi wa-khiftu an yadkhulū madīnata baghdāda
sentences.l: And I went out in their track, coveting the horse, and I did not cease following them, and I am not able (to) reach it, because the slaves (were) strong of the guarding over it, until they reached those lands; and I feared that they would enter the city of Baghdad.
sentences.i: So I went out on their trail, coveting the horse, and kept on their heels, but could never get at it, because the slaves guarded it so closely; until at last they came into these parts, and I was afraid they would reach the city of Baghdad.
sentences.n: fī atharihim, “in their track”. The print runs mā into ziltu (مازلت): mā ziltu, “I did not cease”. tābiʿahum, “following them”, a participle taking an object suffix. lā aqdiru aṣilu, “I cannot reach”, drops the an that Classical needs before the second verb, a common Middle Arabic shape. ḥirṣ ʿalā, “keen care for, jealous guarding of”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا أَنَا أُشَاوِرُ نَفْسِي فِي سَرِقَةِ الْحِصَانِ إِذْ طَلَعَ عَلَيْهِمْ غُبَارٌ حَتَّى سَدَّ الْأَقْطَارَ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā anā ushāwiru nafsī fī sariqati al-ḥiṣāni idh ṭalaʿa ʿalayhim ghubārun ḥattā sadda al-aqṭāra
sentences.l: And while I was consulting my soul about the stealing of the horse, behold, there rose upon them a dust until it blocked the horizons.
sentences.i: While I was still debating with myself how to steal the horse, a cloud of dust bore down on them, so thick that it blotted out the sky on every side.
sentences.n: shāwara nafsahu, “to take counsel with oneself”. aqṭār, plural of quṭr, “region, quarter of the horizon”. Rhyme: ghubār, aqṭār.

sentences.t: فَانْكَشَفَ ذٰلِكَ الْغُبَارُ عَنْ خَمْسِينَ فَارِسًا مُجْتَمِعِينَ لِقَطْعِ الطَّرِيقِ عَلَى التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-inkashafa dhālika al-ghubāru ʿan khamsīna fārisan mujtamiʿīna li-qaṭʿi al-ṭarīqi ʿalā al-tujjāri
sentences.l: And that dust uncovered-itself from fifty horsemen gathered for the cutting of the road upon the merchants,
sentences.i: The dust parted to reveal fifty horsemen banded together to waylay merchants on the road,
sentences.n: inkashafa ʿan, “to clear away from, reveal”. qaṭaʿa al-ṭarīq ʿalā, “to cut the road against”, to rob travellers: the highwayman is a qāṭiʿ ṭarīq.

sentences.t: وَمُقَدَّمُهُمْ بَطَلٌ كَأَنَّهُ الضَّيْغَمُ الْهَرَّاشُ يُقَالُ لَهُ كَهْرْدَاشُ وَلٰكِنَّهُ فِى الْحَرْبِ كَأَسَدٍ يَجْعَلُ الْأَبْطَالَ كَالْفَرَاشِ
sentences.tr: wa-muqaddamuhum baṭalun ka-annahu al-ḍayghamu al-harrāshu yuqālu lahu kahrdāshu wa-lākinnahu fī al-ḥarbi ka-asadin yajʿalu al-abṭāla ka-al-farāshi
sentences.l: and their leader (was) a champion as-if he (were) the lion, the snarling-one, (who) is called Kahrdāsh; but he in the war (is) like a lion (that) makes the champions like the moths.
sentences.i: and at their head was a champion like a snarling lion, called Kahrdāsh, a man who in battle was a very lion and scattered heroes like moths.
sentences.n: muqaddam, “one set in front”, the leader of a band. ḍaygham, “lion”, a poetic word; harrāsh, “fierce, given to snarling and biting”, properly of dogs. Rhyme: harrāsh, Kahrdāsh, farāsh. wa-lākinnahu, “but he”, makes no real contrast here and is best taken as “and indeed”. ka-al-farāsh, “like moths”: helpless and scattered, an image from the Qurʾān (101:4), where people on the Day of Judgement are “like scattered moths”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
